Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum trenches, which display a unique gapless quantum regime when the thickness falls within a particular range.  This research was applied to trench structures consisting of a thin layer at the interface between (111)A HgTe and (111)A CdTe, and (111)B HgTe and (111)B CdTe.  We found that the transport behavior in these trench structures differs significantly, with the (111)A/(111)B heterostructures exhibiting a 10-fold increase in length over which transport becomes conductive.  This finding is attributed to the reverse built-in electric field in (111)B HgTe.  Both theoretical predictions and experimental observations demonstrated that the transport properties of these trench structures are sensitive to applied magnetic field and temperature.  This led to remarkable magnetic field-dependent carrier velocities and temperature-dependent edge channels and 2D bulk regimes.  Our results also demonstrated that edge channels can be created through the proper scaling of trench width in comparison to Fermi velocity.  This research reveals the complex interplay between built-in electric fields, temperature, and magnetic effects on transport properties in HgTe quantum trenches, and suggests that this unique material could serve as a platform for designing novel quantum transport devices.  By combining theoretical modeling and experimental data from scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy, transmission coefficient measurements, and magnetotransport experiments, we gained a comprehensive understanding of this phenomenon.  Our findings have implications for designing magnetic field-controlled edge transport, and we propose possible modifications to trench structures, including the creation of magnetic field-controlled edge channels through the introduction of magnetic impurities or the scaling of trench width, and the integration of edge and bulk carrier regimes through the proper scaling of thickness. We consider a specific type of 2.5-dimensional smooth structure, defined on the product of a torus and an interval, subject to a specific volume constraint. For this class of structures, we demonstrate the existence of an invariant, constructed using a pseudo-holomorphic curve construction similar to that in the context of pseudo-holomorphic curve construction for 4-dimensional structures. This invariant exhibits behavior similar to that of the Chern-Simons function for 4-dimensional structures, and it serves as a critical component in defining the quantum invariant of a linked set of torus knots within a region of space. The volume constraint is also utilized to ensure the invariant's divisibility properties are maintained, and it enables us to establish connections between the invariant and the volume of the knots' link. Additionally, we provide computational evidence for the divisibility of certain volume-restricted invariants of knot links, and we demonstrate the relationship between these invariants and the Witten integral. This integration approach can be applied to links composed of multiple torus knots. The most notable example included in the appendix is the 10-torus knot link, defined as the union of three torus knots with distinct radii. This particular case involves a previously unreported integration path and confirms that the volume-restricted invariants of the 10-torus knot links are divisible by 10 through numerical means. The method used to study the 10-torus knot link may also be applied to other links of this type. The development of this research was supported in part by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number JP18K12724. The underlying problem and the approach used to study it have connections to both mathematical and physical contexts. The problem itself is related to the volume-restricted invariants of the 4-dimensional instanton sector, and it involves a specific constraint on the four-dimensional space's volume. In the physical context, this problem can be interpreted as examining the properties of a system composed of a set of free particles moving within a limited volume. When this system is compared to the semi-classical regime, it exhibits a similar behavior, as seen in the context of the Chern-Simons function for 4-dimensional structures. The approach used to study the 10-torus knot link involves a combination of analytical and numerical methods, and it utilizes the Witten integral as the starting point. To accurately determine the context of words with multiple meanings, it is common to rely on dictionaries that provide additional information. This problem, known as Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD), has significant implications for applications like natural language processing, where words with the same name hold distinct meanings. To enhance the performance of a state-of-the-art pre-trained language model in WSD, we propose integrating glosses from dictionaries into the context of words to enhance the model's knowledge. By experimenting with different dictionary entries and selecting the most suitable ones, we found that using BERT-derived senses as a standard for gloss selection leads to a 2% reduction in error rate compared to a baseline approach where no glosses are used. Furthermore, incorporating the most relevant glosses into the model results in an even higher error rate reduction, of 4% overall. This strategy can be applied to other WSD tasks by leveraging numerous free resources available, such as the WordNet dictionary. The code for this project is available online at github.com/ghrua/Word-Sense-Disambiguation.

This study explores expressions for the reciprocal gamma function in terms of integral definitions, extending existing formulas and incorporating regularization techniques to address issues of divergence and singularity. A specific transformation of an integral representation of the reciprocal gamma function is derived, and comparisons are made with other established formulas in the literature. Furthermore, a new representation of the Euler-Mascheroni constant $\gamma$ is obtained by applying these formulations to the Digamma function and its regularized integral equivalent. A notable relation between the regularized integral and the sum of an infinite series is also established, providing insight into the connection between integrals and series in the context of the gamma function and its derivatives. A proposed modification of the definition of the gamma function is also discussed, along with a discussion of the uniqueness of this definition and the characteristics of its derivative. A comprehensive examination is thus presented of various integral formulations of the gamma function, complete with proofs and numerical validation of these formulas. A software function for calculating the gamma function based on these formulations is also developed and tested. A comparison with the standard algorithm for the gamma function demonstrates the novelty of these integral formulations, which offer increased precision at the cost of extended computation time. A connection between the proposed definition of the gamma function and the Weierstrass elliptic function $\wp(z)$ is also introduced, along with a discussion of the possible extension of this relation to positive characteristic. A generalization of the Riemann zeta function, defined as the ratio of two integral representations of the reciprocal gamma function, is also presented, as is a determination of the poles of this generalized zeta function. A numerical calculation of the coefficient of the logarithmic term in the asymptotic expansion of this generalized zeta function at the point $s=1$ is then provided, followed by an examination of the possible extension of this result to positive characteristic. A numerical calculation of the absolute value of the discriminant of the derivative of the gamma function is provided, along with a discussion of the implications of this result for the algebraic nature of the Euler-Mascheroni constant $\gamma$. To achieve this, we investigate proton-lead data at 39 TeV through lead-lead collisions at 39 TeV as well as minimum bias proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV as references. Given the limited information available, we assume the top quark couples to the bottom quark via strong interactions and use multi-variable decisions trees to detect top quark generations. To differentiate the $t\bar{b}$ and $t\bar{s}$ generations, a specific long-range correlation between the most forward and central particles is observed, which could be utilized, along with production ratio estimates, to identify these generations. Furthermore, we find that searching for same-charge top quark pairs at higher transverse momenta may indicate the $t\bar{s}$ generation, whereas the $t\bar{b}$ generation predominates at lower transverse momenta. To differentiate the $t\bar{b}$ and $t\bar{s}$ generations, we propose using lead-lead data at 39 TeV, given its larger collision energy, which could facilitate discovery of the $t\bar{b}$ generation via same-charge top quark pairs at the LHC. This study focuses on key aspects of cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance filling models, the support task was proposed, which includes both filling and linking sub-tasks. Research reveals that supporting filling models with linking sub-tasks, or simply linking models, can significantly improve performance. A robust framework incorporating both filling and linking models was then developed to tackle both sub-tasks. The framework consists of a filling model to fill in values and a linking model to link schemas, with a joint loss function that combines filling and linking loss functions using a weighting factor. The proposed framework was further explored with different weighting factors, revealing that a self-reinforced weighting factor leads to optimal results. Experimental evaluations showed that the proposed framework outperforms baseline models in various evaluation metrics. Furthermore, the self-reinforced weighting factor led to improved performance, with overall results indicating that value filling and schema linking are highly interdependent sub-tasks that significantly benefit from each other. Given a metric space $(M, d)$ and a given homotopy class of maps from a unit disk to $M$, we can consider the subset of maps that have minimal area within that homotopy class. However, since area and homotopy are defined in terms of distances, they can be indirectly determined through the composition of the map in question, making them equivalent to evaluating the intrinsic properties of this composition alone. Therefore, determining area becomes a classification problem based solely on the topological properties of the composition, rather than its geometric characteristics. As such, when examining spaces defined by continuous functions from the unit disk to itself under homotopic equivalence, we can treat them as topological spaces in their own right. Consequently, we can employ established tools from the study of these spaces, including the fundamental group and the compactness of certain subspaces, to investigate the category of surfaces with given boundary properties within these spaces. Specifically, we can use these tools to establish the correctness of a long-standing conjecture of the renowned mathematician Jean-Fernand Pierre originally proposed in 1981. Furthermore, we can demonstrate that, under certain conditions, a particular category of surfaces with specified boundary properties is consistent across all spaces defined by continuous functions from the unit disk to itself under homotopic equivalence, making it compatible with the concept of homotopy group. Lastly, we can provide a more general classification of these surfaces based on their intrinsic properties, including both topological and geometric characteristics. Additionally, we can offer a solution to another problem of Jean-Fernand Pierre related to the composition of maps from the unit disk to itself and the distribution of their respective areas. Lastly, we can offer a general classification of the surfaces in question, including both the scenario where the space defined by continuous functions from the unit disk to itself under homotopic equivalence is compact and the scenario where it is not compact. We introduce a compact function format called Brief Functions (BFs) to represent graphical models, which significantly accelerates the computation of most likely explanations for exact Maximum a Posteriori Estimation and exact Maximum Margin Estimation. We also find this representation useful in reducing the complexity of optimization problems within graphical models, and show that it enables efficient use of existing exact algorithms. Furthermore, we demonstrate that BFs can be created from initial factors in a graphical model, and that these RFs preserve the structural information contained within the original factors. We also introduce a new algorithm called CPLEX from Bottom Up (CFBU) that utilizes BFs to enhance the performance of existing exact optimization algorithms for graphical models. CFBU is a bottom-up approach to problem solving that leverages the simplicity of BFs to eliminate unnecessary subproblems and nodes during optimization, thus significantly reducing both memory usage and the time required for computation. We compare our CFBU algorithm to a standard state-of-the-art optimization package on a collection of randomly generated models and find that it levers a much smaller memory footprint of up to 16 times, and also reduces computation time of up to 14 times. We also analyze the relationship between the complexity of models and the corresponding BF graphs, and show that this relationship can be captured through a new metric called Tree Depth. We propose several approaches to further improve CFBU, including the use of domain-specific knowledge to limit the scope of BFs, and the development of more advanced algorithmic techniques to enhance the efficiency of BF-based optimization. We anticipate that our contributions will be particularly useful in addressing challenges associated with memory-intensive industrial-scale graphical models. We provide our code and model generator at: \url{http://www.cse.ust.hk/~changxing/BF}.

However, PPEP is computationally expensive and its high implementation cost is a significant drawback. To make testing more efficient, we also established a threshold for reducing the number of permutations used in PPEP, while minimizing the information lost about the model's performance. Lastly, PPEP source code is available for public use on GitHub. The fabric space $WF_M$ associated with a given manifold $M$ was introduced by Barrett to provide a framework for constructing natural invariants. This space contains the fundamental class $[M]$ and is defined by a set of local rules that treat the points of $M$ as sources of geometric expansion. A specific method for constructing the fabric space of a simplicial complex is also explained in this paper. Furthermore, an analogy with the Baas--Bott-Tameri construction is drawn, and the paper also delves into the relationship between fabric spaces and the abstract construction of the Grothendieck--Hurewicz map. Additionally, a natural transformation from the fabric space of a simplicial complex to the abstract construction of the Grothendieck--Hurewicz map is proposed. Lastly, the paper concludes by examining the scenario in which the simplicial complex is constructed from the Grothendieck--Hurewicz map and discussing its implications, and it also explores the relationship with the combinatorial definition of the fabric space, ending with an open problem regarding the connectivity of the resulting abstract space.

This research investigates double Higgs production in TeV range $e^+e^-$ colliders, focusing on its sensitivity to beyond the Standard Model Higgs interactions. Initially, we consider the Standard Model plus an omni-effective Field Theory, which provides a comprehensive description of Effective Field Theories. However, a more tailored analysis is conducted for individual Effective Field Theories, such as those that modify the Higgs self-coupling, prevent Higgs decay into gluons, or assign Higgs couplings to third-generation fermions. We explore these individual scenarios at various $e^+e^-$ collider energies with different polarization settings. Our primary interest lies in the response of double Higgs production to changes in BSM Higgs interactions. We achieve this by analyzing the ratio of double to single Higgs production as an indicator of BSM Higgs interactions. Our study covers two main scenarios: (1) $e^+e^-$ colliders with low energy, for which we focus on the response of single Higgs production to BSM Higgs interactions, (2) colliders with high energy, for which we examine the sensitivity to BSM Higgs interactions at the level of effective Field Theories. In the low-energy context, we explore two scenarios with 150 GeV and 250 GeV center-of-mass energy, while in the high-energy context we examine two scenarios with 250 GeV and 350 GeV. We find that at the level of individual Effective Field Theories, the ratio of double to single Higgs production exhibits a distinct response to BSM Higgs interactions, offering a clear signature for certain BSM Higgs interactions, such as the change in Higgs self-coupling or the Higgs-fermion couplings to third-generation fermions. On the other hand, at the level of effective Field Theories, we can also provide a precise definition of the ratio of double to single Higgs production that is insensitive to BSM Higgs interactions, achieving a 10\% accuracy with 10 femtobarns of data at an $e^+e^-$ collider with a 250 GeV center-of-mass energy. We conclude that $e^+e^-$ colliders offer a versatile platform for investigating Effective Field Theories and provide a powerful tool for discovering BSM Higgs interactions. We investigated the drag experienced by a solid cylinder moving through a layer of granular material filled with fluid by performing experiments and numerical analyses. Our study focused on a scenario where the fluid fully surrounds the cylinder and we found that drag forces can differ significantly, a phenomenon known as drag asymmetry. Our research revealed that the direction of greater drag force is dependent on the velocity of the cylinder's movement. When the cylinder moves slowly, greater drag is exerted on the front side, but as it moves faster, more drag is applied to the rear side. Our further investigation highlighted that the deeper the layer of granular material, the drag asymmetry becomes less noticeable. Moreover, our findings demonstrated that drag asymmetry can be influenced by the angle at which the cylinder moves, becoming more pronounced in some cases. Our analysis of experimental data alongside numerical simulations using a two-dimensional model also known as a biviscous model, enabled us to gain a deeper understanding of the complex interactions occurring between the cylinder, the layer of granular material, and the surrounding fluid. Our study also highlighted the effects of different layer depths on the model's predictions of drag asymmetry. A critical issue in using Krylov methods for large systems of equations arising from discrete partial differential equations is the loss of solution accuracy, particularly in the presence of steep gradients. This research focuses on Krylov solutions to certain systems of equations that result from discretizing particular types of PDEs, specifically those involving PDEs with steep gradients and high Anisotropic Anisotropy Factors (AAFs). To address this challenge, a new concept, the Anisotropic Anisotropy Factor (AAF), is introduced to measure the anisotropy of a discretization matrix and various bounds on AAF are derived, depending on the properties of the underlying differential operator and the shape of the computational domain. These anisotropy measures can be interpreted as indicators of the anisotropic effects on a discretization, such as the effects of anisotropic diffusion, anisotropic elliptic operators, and the methods of distributed and non-uniform grid generation. To mitigate the loss of precision, this research introduces a new approach based on interpreting the Krylov solution as an operator that acts on the initial guess, allowing for the application of shape-preserving properties to this operator rather than the solution itself. This leads to the development of a set of conditions that ensure the preservation of a monotonicity property for the Krylov solution, and provide routes to overcome the challenges of precision loss, including the escalation of anisotropy within the context of adaptive grid methods. Finally, numerical examples are presented to illustrate the application of these theories to hyperbolic and convection-diffusion PDEs, including a test case involving the transport of a scalar field and the Bousques-Jolion shock flow problem. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on accurate non-rigid registration between three-dimensional volume data and real-time surface scans. Although machine learning-based methods have achieved high precision, their scalability and real-time performance are yet to be demonstrated. In contrast, biomechanical models, which incorporate physiological properties of tissues, provide a precise and physically meaningful means of registration but are generally too computationally intensive for practical use. We combine the advantages of these two approaches by developing a real-time biomechanical model for registration, tailored to specific surgical applications with minimal setup required. This approach utilizes a simple finite element model that leverages the stability and precision of biomechanical methods, allows for real-time performance, and demonstrates effective alignment between volumes and surface scans. Our model has been assessed for its precision, scalability, and ease of setup, yielding promising results for general surgical use cases. Moreover, this method has been applied to the challenging problem of abdominal soft-tissue navigation, where it has shown a notable improvement over existing state-of-the-art approaches. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/surgery8416/Zero-Order-FEM. [Abstract text]

Acquiring extensive datasets for training models in new applications can be challenging due to data collection and labeling costs. The Self-Taught Learning framework addresses this issue by enabling models to be fine-tuned on a new dataset after initially training on a different one. In the context of scene flow estimation, correlating stereo images with corresponding three-dimensional points enables the reconstruction of dynamic natural scenes. However, training models on stereo images and evaluating their performance on scene flow is misleading due to the loose connection between the two topics. Current self-taught learning approaches fail to address this issue, simply relying on the neighbors of past training points to guide the model towards better performance. In contrast, we propose a novel method, Adversarial Metric Training for Self-Taught Scene Flow, that leverages an adversarial contrastive learning technique to reweight the model's parameters based on an objective metric unrelated to the input data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by training a model on the KITTI stereo image dataset and evaluating its performance on the SIFT flow dataset, obtaining a 9.3 mm three-dimensional flow estimation error on the KITTI test dataset. We also analyze the proposed method's robustness in relation to other self-taught learning techniques and various parameters of the adversarial contrastive learning technique. Finally, we discuss the generalization of our approach to other computer vision tasks. The research also generalizes the asymptotic stability results for the ground state of the focusing Klein-Gordon equation from its original form to a more expansive scenario. A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, a combination of high-resolution imaging techniques and rigorous statistical analysis, including a calculation of dispersion, was employed to examine IKNM in the developing zebrafish retina. Our findings reveal that retinal neuron migration follows a consistent patterns during early stages of development, yet as the retina matures, this pattern disrupts and movement becomes unpredictable. Our data also indicate that retinal neuron migration becomes less consistent and more random in older embryos, which is reflected in a significant increase in the dispersion of nuclear movement. Our analysis further reveals that the source of this increased dispersion is the growing age of the neuron nuclei themselves, which contributes to the breakdown of the IKNM pattern. Our work demonstrates that a widely observed phenomenon of IKNM in developing neural tissues is, in fact, a dispersive process, and as such, it is a critical factor in shaping the complex layering patterns observed in these tissues. Furthermore, our findings provide a framework for studying the underlying mechanisms of IKNM, including the role of nuclear age, that can be applied to other developing neural tissues. The general importance of this research is highlighted by the widespread occurrence of IKNM in developing neural tissues, where a similar dispersive process may contribute to the formation of layering patterns observed in various parts of the brain. The data and analysis presented in this study have been made publicly accessible to facilitate further investigation of this widespread phenomenon of neural development. The underlying code has been deposited in a public repository located at https://github.com/JamesBuckley95/IKNM, while the related imaging data has been deposited in a public repository located at http://www.emblab.org/datasets/retina/. The code and imaging data described in this study may be used to reproduce the results and figures presented in this paper, as well as to investigate IKNM in the developing retina and other neural tissues. The findings of this research have implications for models of neural tissue layering, particularly dynamic agent-based models, and may be applied to other developing neural tissues, such as the cerebral cortex, by considering the role of nuclear age in contributing to the IKNM pattern. The dispersiveness of IKNM may also provide an explanation for the irregular layering observed in certain parts of the brain, such as the temporal lobe, and may be influenced by environmental factors

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states and orbits of small asteroids. As a result, their rotation periods can change over time, and this phenomenon can be the primary driver of retrograde rotation in some asteroids. Previously studied asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro all exhibit short rotation periods that are unlikely given their shapes and bulk densities. By modeling the rotational evolution of these asteroids, we found that their rotation rates likely increased over time due to YORP, causing them to break through the 2:1 spin-orbit resonance. This pattern is unique as there are only a few known cases where increased deformation leads to faster rotation. Furthermore, this phenomenon may be essential in explaining the presence of retrograde rotation in some asteroids. The precise measurement of Geographos's shape through light curves obtained during a 2006 flyby is a crucial confirmation of this model, which was previously developed using ground-based data. If this model is accurate, then YORP's total average strength over its lifetime can be calculated as approximately 5.8 arcseconds per century squared, which is a significant figure that carries minimal uncertainty. The expected shape of Geographos can be inferred from this data, revealing that its shape is similar to that of the asteroid 21 Antios, which is shaped like an elongated ellipsoid. The predicted dimensions of Geographos's shape are approximately 9.5 x 7.5 x 4.5 kilometers. In this context, regular functions from formal sequences to formal power series are redefined. This new definition enables the translation of regular functions into computational expressions. Previously, such conversions were limited to the domain of formal series. This change also extends the concept of regular functions to infinite sequences. Currently available regular functions can be straightforwardly applied to infinite sequences, and a method for creating new regular functions from computational expressions has been developed. These computational expressions can then be converted back into the original context of formal series for comparison with the original regular functions. This new framework is demonstrated with basic regular functions like derivation, integration, and Padé approximation. In addition, a set of rules for creating regular functions from scratch has been established, using the example of Shannon information. This new framework is based on the mathematical principles of regular functions, series, and sequence analysis. The underlying algebraic and analytic structures are represented using an object-oriented approach, and the sequence analysis component is represented by a state chart. The mathematical foundations of regular functions, series, and sequence analysis are reviewed in the appendix. To address information exchange limitations in nonlinear systems, control theorists use attainable sets, containing the possible states reachable through the system given a limited amount of input. Abundant methods are available for calculating these sets for first-order systems, but only a few techniques are effective for nonlinear first-order systems and nearly no solutions exist for second-order systems. In this research, a limited amount of time $T$ within which the system can be driven from an initial state $x_0$ to a target state $x_1$ is modeled using a variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, resulting in the solution $V(x,T)$, which determines the attainable set $\{x \in \mathcal{R}^n \,|\, d(x, \Gamma_T) \leq 0\}$ at time $t=0$. The method involves breaking down the system into independent components, calculating the value function $V_i$ for each component over the time interval $[t,T]$, and then combining these results to obtain the attainable set $\{x \in \mathcal{R}^n \,|\, d(x, \Gamma_T) \leq 0\}$ at time $t=0$. A numerical solution for $V_i$ is also presented, based on the composition of local solution pieces obtained using dynamic programming. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through simulations of a range of systems, including double-degree of freedom systems. The results show that the method can successfully calculate the attainable sets for these systems, even with limited accuracy due to the discrete time-step calculations. The method provides valuable insights into the complex behavior of these systems, and the simulations show that the solution is robust, with the attainable sets at each time step closely approximating the calculated surfaces. The method can be improved by increasing the number of time steps used in the calculations, which would further enhance the accuracy of the results. The research also explores the connection between the attainable sets and the system's phase space, revealing the regions of the phase space that are accessible to the system within a limited time frame. The method provides valuable insights into these regions, which are crucial for understanding the system's dynamics and identifying its unstable periodic orbits. Humans naturally distinguish between living and non-living objects and exhibit a distinct cognitive response to them. Studies have shown that the ventral temporal cortex, particularly the lateral portion, responds differently to animacy than to other visual characteristics, though the basis for this distinction remains unclear. A recent theory suggests that the way people perceive the shape of objects is the foundation of the animacy arrangement in the VTC, as supported by both neuroimaging and behavioral evidence from various experiments. According to this perspective, the VTC's response to the shape of objects is a critical factor in determining their perceived animacy, and the resulting animacy arrangement is a key component of the cortex's representation of the world. A recent study manipulated 3D objects' shape and presence in computer-generated scenes to observe the VTC's response and found that the cortex's response to the same shape depended on whether it was part of a living or non-living object, and that this contrast was independent of the complex stimuli in which the objects were embedded. The study also discovered a specific region within the VTC, known as the animacy cluster, that distinguishes between living and non-living objects based on their intrinsic properties alone. Furthermore, the discovery of the animacy cluster provides a novel foundation for understanding the complex and multifaceted nature of the VTC's response to the world around us. The study's findings have significant implications for various applications including the artificial creation of living beings in computer-generated scenes and the detection of living objects in real-world environments. The prevalence of the VTC's response to shape-based animacy in humans has also been demonstrated across diverse cultures through an online crowd-sourcing experiment that analyzed the classification of living and non-living objects based on their 3D shapes alone. The study has further explored the relationship between the VTC's response to shape-based animacy and the way objects are perceived as three-dimensional entities in space, and has discovered a specific region within the VTC, known as the 3D layout cluster, that distinguishes between living and non-living objects based on their internal structure and spatial configuration alone. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently exacerbated by a small number of highly infectious individuals who have a substantial number of connections, as demonstrated through the example of a person who attends a crowded party and subsequently transmits the disease to a large group of people at a gathering. The crucial role that super-spreaders play in epidemics means that their quick identification and isolation are crucial public health strategies. By integrating a stochastic approach to modeling the occurrence of super-spreader events, our research finds that even a mere 1-10% of daily contact transmissions can lead to a significant increase in the rate of epidemic progression. Our study also reveals that the exponential growth phase of an epidemic is particularly sensitive to super-spreader events, which can be influenced by a wide range of parameters, both systematic and random. The analysis of our research can be applied to a variety of scenarios, including but not limited to epidemics in crowded public places, community-based transmissions, and outbreaks facilitated by mass transportation systems. Our findings underscore the importance of prioritizing intensive control measures in the early stages of an epidemic, in addition to identifying and isolating super-spreaders quickly. Accurate measurements of solar vector magnetic fields are crucial for understanding the behavior of magnetic fields in the sun. The development of advanced magnetometer technologies has led to a plethora of techniques for deriving vector magnetic fields from spectropolarimetric data, with many being made available in an automated format. While such techniques are essential for handling the large datasets generated by modern solar telescopes, the reliability and fairness of these techniques are not well understood, particularly with regard to fairness. In this research, a comprehensive analysis is performed to assess the reliability and fairness of both automated and template-based techniques for deriving vector magnetic fields. The study involves applying these techniques to a vast range of spectropolarimetric datasets via the CESAR code, as well as to data from the Interface Vector Magnetograph, a instrument that directly measures vector magnetic fields. The findings reveal that while both techniques are capable of measuring vector magnetic fields with a magnetic sensitivity of at least 1 kilogauss, they exhibit differences particularly in the alignment of magnetic fields, with some techniques overestimating the degree of alignment by as much as $20^{\circ}$. The study also highlights the presence of bias in the measurements derived from these techniques, particularly for fields above 2.5 kilogauss. In addition, various approaches are explored to alleviate this bias, one of which involves using the LoI threshold as a cleanliness parameter to enhance the accuracy of measurements derived from these techniques. The research emphasizes the need for further development of both automated and template-based techniques for deriving vector magnetic fields, as well as extensive testing of these techniques for reliability and fairness. In the process, the study provides other solar instrumentation developers with useful guidelines that can be applied to their own data analysis tools. The findings of this research are pertinent to a wide range of solar telescopes, including the Advanced Imaging Spectrograph, the European Solar Photon Imaging Vector Magnetometer, and the Solar Optical Universal Polarimeter. The study also addresses the challenge of accurately measuring vector magnetic fields in areas with high magnetic sensitivity, as well as the issue of field alignment in the sun, particularly near sunspots. The research involves a collaborative effort with the DANES, the Interface Vector Magnetograph, the Polarizing Spectrographic Vector Magnetograph, the Biptic Vector Magnetograph, the Full Disk Vector Spectropolarimeter, the High Resolution Full Disk Vector Spectropolarimeter, the Solar Vector Magneto Graph, the Solar Vector Magneto Graph II, the Vector Spectropolarimeter, and the Vector Universal Spectropolarimeter instruments. A neural network-based approach is proposed to address the Hubbard Sign Dilemma in the solution of the Hubbard model. This model poses a significant challenge due to the Hubbard sign problem, which arises when the temperature, a chemical potential, or both are greater than half the bandwidth, causing issues with conventional algorithms. A complex-valued neural network is trained to approximate the thermal expectation values of the model, but must be transformed to handle the Hubbard signs. This is achieved by dividing the complex weights by a factor that varies during the iterations, effectively aligning the weights with the signs. The results show that this method yields accurate energy per site across a range of temperatures and interaction strengths, and can handle both finite and infinite dimensional systems. Furthermore, this algorithm outperforms the exact diagonalization method when the system becomes two-dimensional. However, it falls short when the interaction strength exceeds a certain threshold, requiring the development of a new version that solves the full Hamiltonian directly. This new version, a complex-valued Reversible Jump Adaptive Markov Chain Monte Carlo (RJMCMC), resolves this issue and successfully solves the Hubbard model for all interaction strengths, and in both finite and infinite dimensional systems. This version also reduces the discrepancy when comparing the results of RJMCMC with exact diagonalization. The proposed methods have been applied to a range of models, including the Hubbard model, the Heisenberg spin chain, and the driven-damped Harper model. The complex-valued neural network-based algorithms can handle both discrete and continuous variables, and these models demonstrate the versatility of this method. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, focusing on tasks with partially shared input structures.
A novel approach, unsupervised retrieval-based augmentation, is proposed to achieve this by utilizing unlabeled samples from the target domain to guide model developments.
This is accomplished by incorporating high-quality descriptions drawn from the target domain via retrieval, which leads to a better-fitting model with increased domain adaptation.
To evaluate this approach, a custom dataset containing diverse text classification scenarios is created, and both abstraction-based and data-driven evaluation methods demonstrate the effectiveness of this strategy across multiple tasks. 
The findings are further validated by comparing the method against strong baselines in an extensive experiment involving 10 distinct classification datasets. 
The code and additional details are available at https://github.com/ghru/Unsup-RFA.

Machine learning models are frequently deployed on sensitive data, thus requiring a differential privacy implementation to provide data privacy. Yet, applying differential privacy to deep learning models is often challenging due to its dependence on sensitive input data for parameter tuning. Current methods largely focus on tuning learning rates and hyperparameters for optimal performance within a private model development framework, rather than addressing the underlying architecture and hyperparameter values. In this research, a novel approach is taken to efficiently tune both conventional hyperparameters and learning rates for differentially private neural networks. A straightforward grid search was utilized to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, resulting in a statement that there is a significant performance gain when tuning learning rates and hyperparameters, showing a mean of 38% improved accuracy on a average across various differentially private techniques and various network sizes. Furthermore, this research provides a framework for a streamlined and efficient hyperparameter tuning process, encouraging the integration of methods for automatic hyperparameter adjustment, such as Bayesian tuning. The novel approach and proposed framework were successfully applied to various scenarios, including both basic and advanced configurations, and the related code is available for public use. The rapid spread of COVID-19 globally led to China experiencing a significant surge in digital rumors, which exacerbated challenges in preventing and controlling the virus transmission. To better understand the structure and influence of these rumors, a data set was collected from the typical microblogging platform Weibo, resulting in 582 individually identified digital rumor cases from January 20th to February 29th, 2020. By categorizing the content, identifying key characteristics, and analyzing posts related to each rumor, researchers gained insights into the patterns and behaviors of rumor dissemination. Furthermore, an analysis was conducted of the geographical distribution, online engagement, and temporal development of the rumors, in addition to assessing factors that contributed to their dissemination, such as local health measures, weather, and holiday influences. By examining the data, researchers found that the distribution of rumors conform to the laws of Zipf, and that their dissemination can be described using a combination of the SIR model, with key factors influencing spread, incubation period, and isolation policies. By incorporating the impact of Chinese culture and the role of internet influencers, a better understanding is gained into the complexities of digital rumors. To further alleviate the problem of COVID-19 related digital rumors, recommendations are made to enhance surveillance, improve evaluation methods, and implement targeted counter-measures. This research can serve as a foundation for future studies of COVID-19 related digital rumors, as well as provide practical insights for the platforms and authorities responsible for managing them. This research can also contribute to the broader understanding of the dynamics of rumor dissemination, by providing an analysis of the underlying mechanisms and factors that influence the spread of information online. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered, utilizing panoramic scans of planetary nebulae due to their widespread nature and well-defined luminosity. A planetary nebulae luminosity ratio can be determined from observations of a galaxy's center, sufficiently accurate to calculate a autonomous distance estimate. This method is particularly effective for galactic populations like ellipticals, where bright planetary nebulae can be identified in vast numbers. A previous study covering the central region of the Fornax cluster used this method to determine a distance modulus of 10.78 ± 0.05 (statistic) ± 0.05 (systematic) for a planary nebulae luminosity ratio of 3.05 ± 0.15 (statistic) ± 0.3 (systematic). This result is in agreement with previous measurements obtained using other methods. A comprehensive database of planetary nebulae has been created through the Fornax3D survey, incorporating 4576 detected planetary nebulae within the central region of the Fornax cluster galaxy cluster with luminosities spanning a range of 2-4 log, accurately determined positions with a 1.5 arcsec precision, and individual stellar masses and metallicity for host galaxies. This information, combined with luminosity ratios and a reliable luminosity function for planetary nebulae, enables a precise evaluation of the distance to the galaxies. This has been accomplished for 13 galaxies in the Fornax cluster, with a median precision of 1.5 mag, except for one galaxy with a median precision of 2.4 mag. This approach has been applied to a range of galaxies with different mass distributions, leading to a predictable error margin. A planary nebulae luminosity ratio of 3.05 ± 0.15 (statistic) ± 0.3 (systematic) and a luminosity ratio range of 2.5 to 3.5, which includes the standard abundance gradient per gigaparsec, were assumed in this study. This research was applied to observe the distance distribution of galaxies in the Fornax cluster, discovering that the distance distribution of galaxies is consistent with a uniform distribution, although it lacks a precise analysis. A comprehensive database of planetary nebulae, along with detailed analysis and relevant code, has been made available online. This research was conducted by a team of researchers led by R. Monet, with the assistance of many other individuals.

Integrating continuous queries into streams is efficient with stream management systems like Lagrange, yet applying these systems to temporal data streams is not common practice among top-rated database management systems. In contrast to static queries that are widely adopted within popular databases. In order to make stream management systems a standard part of leading databases, their performance must be brought in line with that of current database management systems. To address this challenge, a high-performance stream processing engine for regular streams has been designed with a focus on efficient execution and easy implementation. The engine, named LifeFlow, achieves superior performance, surpassing popular databases like MySQL and PostgreSQL by an average of 3 times and 2 times respectively in various benchmark tests. LifeFlow also possesses a modular design, both in terms of its architecture and API, allowing easy integration into leading databases with a low overhead of around 100 lines of code. The capabilities of LifeFlow have been thoroughly evaluated in a range of applications, including complex real-world scenarios, with favorable results. LifeFlow is now available as an open-source project under the Apache License. The performance-gaining techniques employed in LifeFlow are also relevant to existing stream management systems and can be utilized as a benchmark to evaluate the efficiency of such systems. In addition to its functional value, LifeFlow can serve as a reference implementation for researchers seeking to evaluate the performance of stream management systems or to assess the efficiency of various stream management systems using LifeFlow as a standard. The development of LifeFlow has also been used to improve the performance of the Lagrange system, resulting in an enhanced version called LagrangeLife. The latter supports weighted regular streams, inherits the design principles of Lagrange, and features a more efficient execution model with a 30% improvement in performance compared to its predecessor. LagrangeLife is now available as an open-source project under the Apache License. When applying deep learning models for classification tasks, it is commonly observed that selecting an appropriate loss function is crucial, as it significantly affects the performance and robustness of the model. In reality, loss functions used in practice often deviate from the standard cross-entropy due to data processing issues, leading to better results. This study investigates the implications of loss function modification on the selected neural network model, focusing on its structured output properties. We demonstrate that loss function alteration can be analyzed in terms of its impact on the model's predicted outputs, rather than the learned features. By doing so, we identify that modifying the loss function is equivalent to modifying the training data, which in turn is equivalent to performing a specific transformation on the target variables. We further show that loss function alteration affects the model's performance in a data-dependent manner, which can be validated through experiments using real-world datasets. Additionally, we provide a theoretical explanation for why changing the loss function often leads to overfitting, which is caused by changing the model's target distribution, leading to a model that is too complex to effectively generalize. We conclude that loss function alteration is a data-dependent issue that requires careful consideration, and it is essential to evaluate models on a held-out set of data to ensure they are resistant to such changes. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis. A key outcome of this research is the prediction of a sharp peak in specific heat coefficient that can result from a Lifshitz transition, with a characteristic width driven by electron-electron interaction. This research introduces a new delay-enhancement technique that raises the required bit duration to the point that it exceeds the average bit duration of coherent methods, such as CPM, making it more difficult to confuse. We apply the quantum potential approach to the Klein-Gordon field theory within a quantum cosmological framework. By utilizing the Schrödinger picture, we derive the equation of motion for a scalar field in a closed system, incorporating both quantum effects and temperature influences. Subsequently, we determine the mean density and pressure of the spacetime, defining these quantities in the compressible universe model. By analyzing these results, we demonstrate that the quantum potential and conformal coupling play a significant role in determining the spacetime's density and pressure. Furthermore, we show that the ratio of the quantum potential to the energy density tends toward zero as the temperature increases. In the context of the compressible universe model, we find that the average density and pressure of the spacetime exhibit a negative gradient, suggesting that the spacetime's density and pressure must both approach zero within a finite distance from the universe's center. This finding has important implications for the fundamental nature of the quantum compressibility of spacetime. In the course of our analysis, we also derive an expression for the average energy density of the spacetime, given the mean energy density operator, and demonstrate that the spacetime's density must be proportional to the average energy density when the coupling is conformally zero. Additionally, we show that the quantum compressibility of the spacetime is influenced by temperature-driven fluctuations between the universe's empty and filled states. Finally, we discuss the relationship between the quantum potential approach and the Wheeler-DeWitt equation within the quantum cosmological framework, and the implications of using the quantum potential in the Schrödinger picture in place of the Wheeler-DeWitt equation in analyzing the spacetime's density and pressure in closed systems. In the process, we offer a more comprehensive analysis of the influence of temperature-driven fluctuations on the spacetime's density and pressure, and provide a mathematical expression that describes this effect. Furthermore, we derive an expression for the free energy of the spacetime and demonstrate that the quantum compressibility of the spacetime is influenced by temperature-driven fluctuations between the universe's empty and filled states. In the context of the compressible universe model, we show that the spacetime's density and pressure must both approach zero within a finite distance from the universe's center and argue that the fundamental nature of the spacetime's compressibility is deterministic, in contrast to the semiclassical cosmological framework based on the Wheeler-DeWitt equation, which suggests that the spacetime's density and pressure may fluctuate between the universe's empty and filled states. However, implementing such a method poses challenges, including the need for a compatible optimizer and a suitable attention mechanism to handle imbalances in the frequency of speech and text data. Another issue arises from the fact that large language models are typically trained on massive text datasets that include numerous synonyms of the desired targets. To address these challenges, a proposed model called Speech-Text Aware Transformer (STAT) develops an attention mechanism that focuses on both speech and text on different layers, reducing the disparity between their frequencies. Additionally, STAT incorporates a technique called sequence mask cross-entropy, which helps prevent the model from generating synonyms. When evaluated on InConvE and Switchboard, STAT demonstrated significant improvements in word error rates (WER), achieving 8.32% and 19.11% gains respectively. This article uses combinatorial and analytic methods to analyze the set of natural numbers represented by the sum of their digits in base $k$, added to a shift of $k$. We are interested in the structure of this set for a given $k$, and how it changes as $k$ increases from 2 to infinity. Our analysis focuses on the number of elements in the set, its smallest element, the largest element, and the elements' asymptotic behavior in the context of $k$. We establish a lower and upper limit for the number of elements in the set, show that the smallest element is greater than $k-1$, the largest element is less than $k^2$, and determine the asymptotic behavior of the set's smallest and largest elements as $k$ increases to infinity. We also explore the relationship between this set and the interval $(k^2-k)\sqrt{k}/2$ when $k$ is an even number greater than 2. Additionally, we provide some recursive formulas and explicit descriptions for the set's asymptotic characteristics in the context of $k$. Our results build upon previous work by J.A. Deano and V. Requardt, and we discuss how our methods differ from theirs. Our main tool for analyzing the set's asymptotic characteristics is the combinatorial concept of parking functions, and we outline an alternative proof of the formula for the number of elements in the set using this approach. Finally, we address some open questions related to the set's asymptotic characteristics in the context of $k$. The article also includes a discussion of the implications of our results for random variables represented by the sum of their digits in base $k$, added to a shift of $k$, and provides some background information on parking functions, random variables represented by the sum of their digits in base $k$, and the interval $(k^2-k)\sqrt{k}/2$. We end by outlining the paper's structure and providing a glossary of the terms used. The main paper consists of an introduction followed by five sections, and we offer some commentary on the sections' content. The article also includes a bibliography of 25 references. This study examines the electronic conductance of superconducting NbN nanowires as they transition through 2e packets of charge, a phenomenon known as the Coulomb blockade. By investigating how gates influence the behavior around the Tobridge, a barrier that prevents direct tunneling between the nanowire and an external electrode, we observed two distinct scenarios. When the nanowire's end is close to the edge of superconductivity, we found two separate junctions that each complete a full 2e cycle independently, resulting in four possible phases and aligning with our measurements of critical current densities. However, when the nanowire's end is further inside the superconducting region, we observed a more complex behavior in which the conductance jumps occur at 1e packets of charge, accompanied by a $\pi$-phase shift between the two ends. One possible explanation for this latter behavior is a quantum phase-jump phenomenon mediated by quasiparticles, although it could also be attributed to the obstruction of 2e tunneling by a trapped pair of quasiparticles. To confirm this, we investigated the duration of one e-jump and found it to be approximately 10-20 ms, a time frame that is significantly longer than the lifetime of non-equilibrium states but still relatively brief. This data supports the idea that 2e tunneling is obstructed and that the nanowire's conductance is regulated by the capture and release of a single quasiparticle, which could be achieved by adjusting the gate to modify the Tobridge and favor a 1e jump over the $\pi$-phase jump phase, thus making the nanowire suitable for use in a sensitive counter for individual quasiparticles. Although this study used NbN nanowires, this phenomenon is likely to occur in other material nanowires and it could be an important feature to consider in a wide range of superconducting quantum devices. This work was conducted using an experimental setup that incorporated a single nanowire in contact with an electrode, connected to a signal generator, an lock-in amplifier, and a controller for the gate electrodes, and the data was analyzed using a script that extracted specific features from the conductance measurements. In this research, the inter-atomic and inter-molecular interaction between orbitals is examined as a key factor for understanding and explaining electronic and lattice behavior in 2D materials made of titanium tercarbide (TiC2). Calculating the material's properties using first-principles calculations, we found that the TiC2 material has an unusual, anisotropic electronic structure characterized by localized and mobile electrons operating in separate orbital planes with varying distances between them. We also observed that the material's anisotropic structure allows for distinct, independent motion of electrons in different orbital planes, reducing the dimensionality of its electronic and phonon states. As a result, we predict unique state transition sequences for this material. Furthermore, our calculations showed that the dimensionless interaction parameter decreases with increasing lattice constant, particularly affecting the dimensional reduction and anisotropic behavior. Consequently, experimental techniques such as angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, scanning tunneling spectroscopy, and Raman spectroscopy can be influenced by the anisotropic electron loss channels and inter-orbital interaction, affecting the interpretation of data. Moreover, theoretical models of TiC2 overestimate the magnitude of inter-orbital interaction when using narrow basis sets, which can be avoided by using projection operators to eliminate redundant orbital components, thus obtaining a more accurate representation of the material's energy and phonon spectra. Lastly, our calculations predicted a unique anisotropic lattice distortion in the high-pressure phase of TiC2, which may be verified through experimental means. In summary, understanding the inter-orbital interaction in TiC2 is crucial for accurately interpreting data from various experimental techniques and theoretical models, which can be achieved through proper dimensionless interaction analysis, accurate basis set selection, and careful consideration of lattice constant effects. This knowledge also provides a foundation for potential applications of this material in quantum technology, given its unique properties and behavior. Understanding how epidemics spread within densely populated environments like public transportation systems is crucial for developing effective public health strategies. The insights gained from this study are relevant to other enclosed, crowded environments. Dungeons and Dragons, a renowned fantasy role-playing game, has seen a significant surge in digital adaptations guided by artificial intelligence dungeon masters. These systems use conversations to guide players through immersive stories and challenging puzzles. In response to the growing popularity of D&D, we present a new approach that teaches AI dungeon masters how to effectively lead digital versions of the game. Our method, built on top of the well-known text-based adventure game framework, uses reinforcement learning to train the master's decision-making process and a combination of natural language processing techniques to refine their storytelling skills. To evaluate our method, we developed a custom assessment metric and a benchmark by which our performance is measured. Our approach surpasses the current state-of-the-art in several key areas, demonstrating substantial improvements in both player engagement and overall game satisfaction. Our code is available at https://github.com/PranavGiorgi/ANDSHANDBOOK.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their functional behavior remains a complex and intriguing topic. Recent studies suggest knots may serve a purpose in protein stability and dynamics, but the specific mechanisms behind this remain unclear. Given the variety of knotting patterns and bending preferences in proteins, a standardized approach is necessary to compare their behavior. In this work, we introduce the Minimax Bridge Length (MBL) metric to analyze the underlying topology of knots in proteins, focusing on the most fundamental property - the connection between loop ends. By applying topological data analysis (TDA) to dynamic changes in proteins, we identified persistent topological features that reflect the static and dynamic properties of knots. Specifically, we found that the topology of knots reveals preferred bending directions and locations, as well as localized changes in knot geometry in response to various conditions. Our results demonstrate the capabilities of a machine learning model trained on TDA features to predict bending preferences simply by looking at the static and dynamic topology of a knot. This approach also reveals the importance of distinguishing between loop ends based on dynamic changes, as it affects the accuracy of bending direction predictions. Furthermore, we found that the topology of knots remains relatively stable under certain conditions, while dynamic changes are concentrated in localized bridge regions. Our findings suggest that condition-dependent changes in knot geometry are often limited to specific areas and that the distribution of non-ambient topological features can indicate the level of native conditions in a protein. Finally, our research highlights the unique structure of protein knots that possess both intrinsic and extrinsic topological properties, and demonstrates how the MBL metric and TDA methods can be applied to predict the physical behavior of knotted proteins based solely on their sequence. Our approach provides a customizable framework for analyzing the complex relationship between protein topology, dynamics, and environment, and offers a theoretical sequence-based prediction of physical behavior that requires further experimental verification. Our data is available online at https://knoldus.shinyapps.io/knoldus_shiny/. Our code is available online at https://github.com/knoldus/protein_knots. A deviation from the standard Goldstone theorem's consequences has been observed in irregular broken symmetries, which are not universally recognized. This paper will illustrate the irregular Goldstone theorem's formulation, its connection to the general goldstone theorem, as well as specific cases where its principles hold or fail, by analyzing a relativistic scalar field theory with Weyl symmetry. Unlike regular goldstone theorems, the irregular version implies that anomalous Ward identities will be violated, resulting in the disappearance of the irremovable delta function term when the initial symmetry is regularized. A direct goldstone theorem, which is a simplified version of the irregular one, can be applied to a $U(2)$ linear sigma model that involves both scalar and fermi fields. This model exhibits both regular and irregular Nambu-Goldstone modes: the regular ones arise from the $U(1)$ symmetry, while the irregular ones arise from the $U(1)$ symmetry that is not linear. The relationship between the irregular goldstone theorem and its direct version is similar to that between the conventional goldstone theorem and its direct version. The irregular goldstone theorem's failure in theories with linearly realized $U(1)$ symmetries, such as QED, is well known. The consequences of Weyl symmetry being pregauged versus exact symmetry are also examined. The principle of the irregular goldstone theorem can be reexpressed in terms of the notion of symmetry breaking, which leads to the concept of "gauge symmetry without goldstone particle". The enrichment obtained from viewing the irregular goldstone theorem through the conventional goldstone theorem's lens is demonstrated by analyzing a $U(2)$ linear sigma model. The relationship between the irregular and direct goldstone theorems' formulations can be applied to other symmetries, such as the conformally invariant theory. Research into epitaxial growth on low-energy surfaces faces a challenge due to a broad category of surfaces falling under the definition. Epitaxial growth can be influenced by various factors including structural, electronic, and chemical alignments between the substrate and layer. To tackle this complexity, a new classification system called the epitaxy map has been devised, taking into consideration the recent development of van der Waals epitaxy. This map can be presented as an epitaxy triangle, representing distinct regions of close-lattice, open-lattice, and high-density states. Distinguishing between these states is crucial as it affects the equilibrium between different epitaxial phenomena including far-lattice, patch, and van der Waals epitoxy. Our research demonstrated that Heusler layers exhibit diverse epitaxial behaviors on a single substrate, from close-lattice pinhole epitoxy to van der Waals epitoxy, influenced by surface preparation and layer density. Consequently, a well-designed experimental setup was utilized to explore the epitaxy of Heusler layers on a graphene/sapphire substrate. Our findings showed that this system is capable of displaying various epitaxial states, from close-lattice to open-lattice and van der Waals epitoxy, facilitated by a range of pressure and temperature conditions that can be controlled to achieve desired epitaxial behaviors. This level of control over epitaxial states is unprecedented and could have a significant impact on the successful growth of Heusler layers used in spintronics and photovoltaic applications. Moreover, this breakthrough also highlights the potential of graphene/sapphire as a versatile substrate for growing layers with complex epitaxial requirements. Our research has been concentrated on Heusler layers, but its findings are relevant to any layer that can grow on graphene/sapphire, including transition metal dichalcogenides, oxides, and II-VI compounds. Our recent discovery has further enriched the epitaxy map by uncovering an unknown region that represents the interplay between close-lattice and van der Waals epitoxy, facilitated by the unique characteristic of Heusler layers' lattice rotation. This finding provides a new avenue for exploring layers with rotated lattices and offers a precise control over lattice rotation without compromising the crystalline quality of the layer. This research has been carried out in an air environment, and the growth conditions have been controlled to achieve layers with a high crystalline quality and well-defined rotaional angles. Our findings have further extended the epitaxy map to include the regulation of lattice rotation in air environments.

This research introduces a novel technique called Multi-Instance Learning from Positive Examples (MILEAGE) to address these challenges by learning a function that as input receives individual positive examples and outputs a set of associated relevant labels. The nature of gamma-rays observed in nearby radio galaxies remains unclear, as their powers exceed predictions by several orders of magnitude. In a new study, we examine if disks powered by magnetic captures could be responsible for these excessive gamma-rays. When a fast-moving magnetic field generates by a spinning black hole interacts with nearby matter, it forms a disk. This type of disk differs from standard accretion disks and can power jets that emit gamma-rays. We applied a theoretical model of magnetic capture disks to the sub-parsec region around a supermassive black hole and studied their impact on gamma-ray spectra. By comparing our results with data from the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, we found that magnetic capture disks and their associated jets emit gamma-rays that could account for the excessive gamma-rays observed in a group of low-power radio galaxies. In fact, these disks are so efficient that they could explain the same amount of gamma-ray power with a third less mass than is currently assumed. However, they do struggle to account for the observed satellite patterns in gamma-rays, which are likely caused by relativistic jets that are present in some of these galaxies. In a second part of the study, we looked at the relationship between gamma-rays and low-energy radiation, finding that gamma-rays are powered by matter that falls into the black hole rather than the surrounding hot gas. This suggests that even if the amount of gas around these black holes decreases, the gamma-rays they produce will continue to power the observed levels of radiation in the surrounding environment. In a third part of the study, we examined the possible locations of gamma-ray emitting disks and found that they could be limited to the sub-parsec region around the black hole, rather than extending further out, which is the current assumption. This is consistent with findings from other observations and could be explained if the magnetic capture disks are powered by the movement of the black hole rather than the movement of the surrounding gas. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate diagnosis relies on the skill level and experience of healthcare professionals, limiting accessibility.  A potential solution involves using machine learning models based on cardiac sound analysis, but these methods often fail in clinical environments due to noise and poor sound quality.  This study aims to overcome these challenges by developing a method to accurately categorize heart sounds in clinical settings.  A short signal length was chosen to make the analysis more robust against rapid degradation of signals, and feature extraction was performed using PCA and LDA to obtain a compact and distinct signal representation.  The effectiveness of this approach was demonstrated on publicly available datasets, and the results showed that it outperforms existing methods in various settings.  Additionally, the analysis was applied to a fictional dataset that simulated real-world heart sound recordings in clinical environments, and it successfully identified all normal and abnormal sound categories with a short signal length, even when there was rapid degradation, noise, and convolutional interference.  The results have the potential to improve accessibility of cardiac auscultation, and they provide a foundation for future research and development of machine learning models based on real-world heart sound recordings.  A discussion on issues and potential solutions for future research is also presented.  A category model, a signal quality assessment method, and a way to correct deformed signals are some of the additional topics explored in this study.  A publicly available framework for heart sound analysis is available at https://github.com/AminRostamiHeart/HeartSoundCategory. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces the FedHealth system, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and develops personalized models via transfer learning on cloud platforms. It incorporates two novel techniques: 1) a federated learning-based activity dataset constructor, and 2) a novel approach called the Federated Transfer Knowledge Structure. This research paper analyzes and compares various methods for optimizing portfolio performance, including those that utilize higher-order moment modifications. Initially, we review the most widely accepted portfolio optimization strategies and the challenges they pose, such as the squaredness issue and lack of diversity in recommended assets. To address these limitations, we divide portfolio enhancement methods into three categories based on the approach used: convex optimization, robust optimization, and the application of higher-order moment constraints. Each method from the literature that falls into these categories is presented within its respective group. We also examine the relationship between some of these methods and provide alternatives to convex optimization-based solutions, such as the use of moment constraints to achieve better diversity in recommended assets. Finally, we discuss a specific scenario in detail to demonstrate the differences in asset recommendations generated by various methods. This paper is intended for academic and professional researchers, asset/portfolio managers, and financial institutions deciding on portfolio performance enhancement strategies. We use a real-world dataset to illustrate the methodology, which can be applied to other datasets in the financial sector. Existing solutions focus on automated testing and are not relevant to the broader context of ASH. Nevertheless, valuable lessons can be extracted from them to contribute to the ASH endeavor. This research focuses on a control problem where the expenditure process is subject to fluctuations and must be managed to maximize long-term expectations under risk. The goal is to determine the most effective control strategy to minimize excess costs while achieving optimal expected results. The study demonstrates the existence of a optimal control approach characterized by a specific "toggle" behavior, where it is beneficial to switch between two distinct control modes. The paper also establishes the uniqueness of the toggle control solution in a broad context. Furthermore, it demonstrates that the risk-neutral expectation can be expressed as the supremum of the expected results of all feasible control approaches. The study also utilizes a real-world example involving the optimal management of carbon emissions taxes to illustrate the results presented. The findings are then verified through numerical analysis of the problem. The paper also offers an approach to solving the static version of the toggle control issue, as well as two alternative formulations of the problem that involve constraining the starting and ending states of the system. The research can be applied to a wide range of fields, including finance, operations research, and environmental management. The paper provides a detailed introduction to the subject, as well as an overview of the methods used and the results obtained. The research can be categorized under the topic of stochastic control theories, particularly risk-sensitive random control systems, and can be further divided into five sections. The paper offers two possible formulations of the toggle control issue, as well as a management example involving the optimal management of carbon emissions taxes.
