Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual merging binary black holes with approximately $10^{-4}$ M$_{\sun}$ masses. As PTA signals are typically modeled, they are assumed to be circularly symmetric, which may limit the accuracy of waveform interpretations. To address this limitation, we developed a method to generate highly accurate (post-Newtonian) PTA signals for binary black hole mergers with significant orbital eccentricity, using an analytical approach rather than numerical methods. By optimizing this approach, we were able to efficiently create a library of PTA signals for eccentric binaries, allowing for effective comparison with actual PTA data. The precision of these generated signals was validated through comparison with actual waveforms, demonstrating that their correlation is extremely high (typically 0.99 or greater). The computational expense of this method was found to be significantly lower than using numerical methods for multiple combinations of PTA arrays and binary merger parameters. As a result, this analytical approach can be used to detect and characterize PTA signals resulting from merging binary black hole mergers with eccentricity, offering a valuable tool for PTA analysts. The accuracy of these signals was further assessed through detection efficiency calculations, which demonstrated that this approach can accurately recover the physical parameters of eccentric binaries, recovering their mass, distance, orbital decay, and spin components with a precision of 1% or better. The next step in this research involves creating analytical models of PTA signals for binary mergers with precessing spins, which will allow for the recovery of spin orientations and potentially open up new avenues for astronomical research. The development of these analytical models has significant implications for PTA analysis, offering a way to recover precision astrophysical information from detected signals with the correct interpretation of their computational expense. The accuracy of these models was assessed through comparison with numerical waveforms, demonstrating that they can recover the frequency characteristics of waveforms with a signal-to-noise ratio of 100 or greater. The computational expense of these models was found to be $10^{6}$ times lower than using numerical methods for similar combinations of PTA arrays and binary merger parameters. We illustrate how the ASEP velocity evolution can be expressed in terms of hydrodynamic coefficients, thereby providing a direct means of achieving a hydrodynamic interpretation for the system. We demonstrate that the velocity procedure is poised to yield a nonlinear Burgers equation when applied to the ASEP, and we illustrate the asymptotic behavior of its associated conservation law. Furthermore, we show that the velocity procedure acts as a destructive operation that removes the next-largest discrete hydrodynamic mode, and we establish that its repeated application produces a sequential hierarchy of discrete hydrodynamic modes. We derive the specific coefficients for the basic ASEP model, the bounded ASEP, and the ASEP with a step initial condition. Lastly, we provide an appendix detailing the application of the velocity procedure to these systems.

A distinguished subset of models incorporating specific factors such as school dynamics, agricultural supply chains, and immigration/emigration trends have been particularly useful in providing valuable insights. Furthermore, this study explores the implications of withdrawing non-essential measures once a significant population immunity threshold is reached. A key observation from our analysis indicates that relaxing such measures during the early stage of the epidemic may lead to catastrophic consequences, whereas withdrawing them later may result in only a gradual increase in case numbers. This finding agrees with the findings from other studies using different methods. We believe that discrete time models offer a more accurate representation of the epidemic dynamics and therefore recommend their use over continuous time models. We also examine the existence of switching curves, the dynamics of the epidemic, and the associated transmission threshold. Furthermore, we investigate the coherence of discrete time models by comparing our piecewise linear discrete time model with a continuous time model involving delays. We analyze the model's dynamics across different epidemic scenarios, including hyperinfectious variants, changing population sizes, and different recovery rates. We also suggest that researchers adopt discrete time models and note the potential dangers of models that overestimate recovery rates. We conclude by proposing a research agenda for modeling outbreaks, including the current COVID-19 epidemic, and recommending further investigation into specific themes. HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. Since the optimal exposure spectrum depends on both the camera hardware and its surrounding environment, we researched how to determine the ideal range and how to process images for HDR production. In this study, mobile HDR technology is examined, and a new approach is presented that utilizes a first-order Tikhonov regularization method to determine the target images' exposure range, followed by image fusion using a technique based on Tikhonov regularization to create a single HDR image. Our scheme's effectiveness was demonstrated through simulations and mobile HDR applications using Nokia and Samsung smartphones. The results show that our method produces higher-quality HDR images compared to existing mobile HDR technologies and captures a wider dynamic range than conventional HDR methods. This paper focuses on developing a sentiment analysis model that can be applied across different languages by using pre-trained multilingual models. We evaluated two different approaches for generating XLSA models: one based on weighted averaging of monolingual models and another involving multi-task training. Our findings indicate that multi-task training yields superior performance compared to the weighted averaging method. We also discovered that sending the hidden representations of BERT instead of the classification outputs for multi-task training leads to better results. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that multi-task training decreases the gap between large-scale languages like Spanish and small-scale languages like Welsh. Our proposed approach surpasses the state-of-the-art methods in multiple assessments, as demonstrated in our experiments. We made all XLSA models and scripts available for public use.

X-ray images contain visual information that can be used to determine the level of lung infection in patients suffering from COVID-19 before their admission to an Intensive Care Unit. To achieve this, we must look at a crucial time period in the pandemic's early stages. With Infections surge and healthcare systems under strain, accurate prediction of high-risk patients is crucial. We examine the image characteristics of patients who did and didn't require ICU treatment and find distinct patterns in lung infection symptoms. Our findings indicate that areas of infected lungs tend to consolidate into solid masses, with the majority of infected areas located in the upper lungs. We also identify an important criterion - the absence of the "crazy pneumonia" feature - which is more prevalent in patients who require ICU treatment. By analyzing these patterns, our research provides a foundation for developing machine learning models that can accurately analyze X-ray images and predict ICU admission for COVID-19 patients. Our results are validated using various machine learning models and illustrate the uniqueness of the pandemic's early stages. Our approach can be applied to future pandemics with similar time periods and imaging characteristics. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghasemipourGhasemi/ICU-COVID19.

The severity of false positives in visual association detection becomes particularly stressful during high activity situations. In scenarios like these, false associations can lead to critical consequences, resulting in accidents, games lost, or simply undesirable outcomes. To address this issue, a new detection framework is proposed that identifies false positives in visual association tasks, particularly those with an open-ended number of categories. The proposed method incorporates an iterative process that removes easily predicted classes, making it harder to find false positives in return. This process is repeated until the model's performance drops below a specified threshold. The proposed framework is demonstrated in experiments using the CLEVR-Viewpoint and the SHAPES datasets, which show that it outperforms existing methods in detecting false positives. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/ghruan/False-Positive-Autoencoder.

Contrary to expectations, these galaxies do not show significant star formation or gas accumulation, unlike many of the galaxies with regular, symmetrical shapes in the same clusters. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the development process for programs utilizing rooted rules, the GP 2 compiler has been enhanced to include a new rule learning technique. This method enables the automatic creation of rooted rules from existing program code, facilitating quick matching and thus a significant reduction in program execution time. Moreover, the EPGP toolset has been developed to support this process, comprising a validator, a rule learner, and a profiler. These tools work together to guarantee the semantic preservation of the original program, efficiently identify areas for optimization, and learn the most appropriate rooted rules. As a result, programs optimized with EPGP demonstrate substantial performance improvements, with a notable increase in programs that can be successfully verified using its validation feature. The EPGP framework and the enhanced GP 2 compiler, along with the rule learning technique, are available under the Apache-2 license and can be downloaded from GitHub. The associated source code and validation results for the examples discussed are also available. The development of EPGP was funded by the Austrian Science Fund (FWF) under the grant number ZK 88. Let's note that GP 2 compiler has a limited community, which is reflected in the paper, and the authors suggest possible ways to expand it. The paper presents an overview of the GP 2 compiler, followed by an in-depth examination of the rule learning technique and the EPGP toolset. The paper then presents case studies highlighting the performance gains achieved with EPGP. The results show that EPGP offers significant performance improvements, with an average verification time reduction of 45% for the tested programs. The paper also presents an analysis of the factors influencing the verification time and offers suggestions for their optimization. The paper concludes by presenting possible directions for further developing the GP 2 compiler and EPGP. Our findings show that a particular set of attributes, which encompass both explicit and implicit characteristics, yields superior results compared to other alternatives. Specifically, a unified framework is presented, featuring five attribute categories that were effectively applied in product descriptions, emotional detection, and celebrity attribute prediction tasks. Due to the sparsity constraints of Lasso, it is effective for continuous variables, but its application on categorical variables is less straightforward. These variables often take the form of one-hot encodings, leading to an exponential increase in model dimensions. This paper presents GLASSEO, a new algorithm that uses a group lasso framework to efficiently handle one-hot encoded categorical variables. By combining a simple and efficient interior-point method with a dedicated strategy for variable selection, GLASSEO outperforms existing alternatives in terms of computational speed and accuracy. The advantages of this algorithm are demonstrated through a range of simulated data sets and real-world examples, including a study on patient outcome predictions based on genetic data. The results show that GLASSEO can typically find better solutions within a given time frame than existing methods, and the algorithm's performance can be further enhanced by a proposed adaptive scaling strategy. The implementation of GLASSEO is an improvement over current solutions and offers a free, open-source alternative for solving a wide range of sparse group modeling problems. In recent years, due in large part to the widespread use of multi-channel recording technology, two-channel speech processing has become a significant area of study. It involves processing two recorded signals of the same speech to produce a single, more accurately reconstructed speech signal. In response to the rising need for fast, real-time speech recovery in various applications, research has also been directed at exploring efficient models capable of processing two channels in a single pass. This paper introduces the Dual-Path Convolutional Recurrent Network (DPCRN), a two-channel speech recovery model that distinguishes its analysis component from its synthesis component, allowing for enhanced speech recovery. The proposed model leverages both convolutional and recurrent networks to process the two recorded signals, one for feature extraction and one for reconstruction, resulting in a 32% reduction in reconstruction error compared to existing models. The DPCRN's simplicity and efficiency are also demonstrated by comparing it to existing models on speech recovery tasks. The proposed DPCRN model achieves a 20% improvement in SI-DRR, a 25% improvement in SI-SERR, and a 32% improvement in MSI-SERR scores. The code for the DPCRN model has been made available online at GitHub.

Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could truly become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become truly entangled with the others if its cavity is highly anti-orthogonal to another cavity, without the need for initial preparation. A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior. Our analysis indicates that both black hole heat capacity and shadow radius exhibit step-like behavior during phase transitions. We also find that the shadow radius can serve as a probe for revealing the thermal profile of black holes in the context of the EPYM gravity framework. This paper introduces a novel task called viewport forecasting in the context of 360-degree virtual travel videos. Given a video with multiple viewpoints, the task predicts the next viewpoint the user will choose based on the video's captions. To address this challenge, we propose a multi-step approach involving two main components. First, we use a viewer-implied rule-based system to generate a grid representing the user's likely viewpoint preferences among all possible views. This grid serves as a proxy for user intent. In the second step, we predict the user's next viewpoint by sampling the peer domain of 2D click-through rates, leveraging the previously constructed grid to filter out impractical suggestions. To evaluate this approach, we collect a dataset consisting of 360-degree virtual travel videos along with their captions and viewer trajectories. This dataset and the proposed methodology for viewport forecasting are available online. Our current methodology achieves a relative improvement of 24.5% in exact match prediction and 18.4% in partial match prediction when compared to the baseline approach. Moreover, we demonstrate the capability of our method to handle real-world datasets by adapting our approach to handle videos without associated trajectories, thus setting a foundation for various applications in the field. The concept of decoupling refers to a technique where a function is divided into two independent components, with one component causing the main problem and the other's impact being negligible. This approach has been widely utilized in various contexts, including partial differential equations, numerical methods, and approximation theories. A notable example is the application of decoupling to a class of functions described by their relationship with the Fourier transform, specifically functions whose Fourier transform contains a region that is far away from the origin and is therefore considered ineffective. The goal of this paper is to explore ways of approximating such functions by dividing the Fourier transform into distinct scales, with the aim of making the decoupling technique more adaptable and effective. A key contribution of this research is to create a framework for approximating functions based on scale-oriented effective uniqueness, which in turn facilitates the development of accurate error estimates for various mathematical operations, such as the maximum value, the $L^2$ norm, and the number of zeros within a specified range. Additionally, this framework enables us to establish upper and lower bounds for a wide range of functions, including those associated with the number of zeros, as well as functions related to the number of distinct pairs of zeros, all within a defined context. A prominent feature of this paper is the introduction of a novel approach to decoupling, which involves dividing the Fourier transform into discrete scales that can be effectively unique, and utilizing this approach to develop approximation theories and error estimates for functions within these scales. A special case of this approach is the development of an error estimate for a class of functions associated with the number of zeros within a defined context, which in turn leads to the establishment of an upper bound for a second class of functions associated with distinct pairs of zeros. A further significant contribution of this research is the creation of a mechanism for adapting the decoupling technique to functions within a context that is based on the relationship between the size of the time domain and the frequency domain, which in turn facilitates the development of approximation theories and error estimates for these functions. The color dipole distribution functions have clear advantages in describing particle production observed at large angles, especially in deep inelastic scattering and hadron collisions. Despite the benefits, researchers have been attempting to connect these functions to quantitative outcomes through the integration of particle distributions. A key obstacle in achieving this integration is the presence of infrared renormalons, which can lead to a shift in the Borel-ordered expansion by an amount equal to the imaginary part of a pole in the complex plane. In this research, the authors focus on identifying the impact of these infrared renormalons on the color dipole partonic distribution functions, particularly the TMD PDF, by analyzing the influence of a specific pole on these functions. A particular bone of contention between researchers is the nature of the pole, described as sharp or rounded, which affects the integration method over particle distributions. In the course of this study, the authors examined the effect of a sharp pole, represented by a singular term in the form $\frac{1}{0}$, on the color dipole TMD PDF in the context of scattering processes at tiny $x$. The analysis revealed that this singular term contributes a constant to the scattering cross-section and also results in the integration over particle distributions being ill-defined. Consequently, the authors resorted to non-perturbative approaches to evaluate the TMD PDF, obtaining a numerical outcome that can be validated against outcomes predicted by the perturbative approach in scattering processes at tiny $x$. The results of this research are reflected in the figures provided, which show the predicted particle production densities in scattering processes at tiny $x$.

We have theoretically examined a novel type of magnetophotonic surface lattices that incorporate orientation-sensitive microstructures made of ferromagnetic and photonic materials, arranged in a two-dimensional vector configuration. Our research indicates that these vector-sensitive magnetophotonic surface lattices possess unique properties that allow them to effectively recognize the polarization of incident light and respond differently to different light polarization modes due to their asymmetrical structures. As a result, we have predicted unusual vector magnetic field distributions that can be localized within the photonic air pockets and exhibit distinct patterns in lattice areas with different orientations. Our findings also suggest that these magnetophotonic surface lattices can be utilized to create highly sensitive, polarization-based optical modes and magnetic field distributions, potentially enabling advanced applications in over-lapping fields of magnetophotronics and metamaterials. Our proposed design can be implemented using current nanofabrication technologies and provides future scalability to be integrated with other materials and components. Our research has been validated through numerical simulations, and we have made the code available for public use. Our work has been further expanded to explore potential extensions in its fundamental principles. Our proposed vector-sensitive magnetophotonic surface lattices have been conceptually categorized into three main designs, each with its own unique features, and we have predicted never-before-seen optical and magnetic field distributions for them. Our research has also predicted distributions of the electric and magnetic fields for all designs, and has further predicted the localization of magnetic and electric fields within the air pockets and dielectric materials, respectively. Our proposed vector-sensitive magnetophotonic surface lattices have also been conceptually expanded to explore potential extensions in their designs, and we have predicted that by moving the air pockets to the dielectric materials, we can localize the electric fields within the air pockets and the magnetic fields within the dielectric materials. To integrate these sublattices, we must align their nodes, which can be difficult due to the lack of information about nodes corresponding to modules with multiplicity one composition factors. In this paper, we demonstrate how to achieve this integration of sublattices from a specific module, C(S_t), where S_t represents a Young diagram of a tableaux t. We then show how to integrate these sublattices to obtain the lattice of submodules for any module with non-multiplicity one composition factors. In real-world scenarios, agents often find themselves in co-observation settings, 
where they observe and learn from the actions of multiple experts with different
specializations. However, most existing methods require expert demonstrations
tailored to specific tasks, which can be impractical or expensive to obtain.
This paper introduces a novel approach, Co-learn, that enables agents to
effectively combine observations of experts performing diverse tasks without
requiring task-specific data. We propose a dual-module framework, featuring
an policy module and a feature module, to achieve co-observation learning.
By sharing a common policy across observed tasks and deriving features for
each situation, Co-learn successfully distills the expertise of observed experts
into a unified representation. This leads to improved performance on unseen
tasks and extends existing limits on co-observation learning. Through our
experiments in complex scenarios with multiple observed experts and varying
scenarios, Co-learn demonstrates significant gains over baseline methods. We
further validate our approach against human-intervention baseline and show
that Co-learn's effectiveness can be optimized by a simple and intuitive
hyperparameter. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChengXuSJTU/Co-learn.

This paper introduces two novel metrics - the cumulative error rate (CER) and the average correction capability (ACC) - to evaluate the performance of error-correction codes. CER measures the total distance encoded by a code, providing a linear scale for code comparisons. ACC, on the other hand, assesses the code's ability to correct errors, considering both the code's structure and the data it encodes. We calculate both CER and ACC for a particular code type - the pulse-addition code (PAC). Specifically, we derive formulas for the average number of correctable errors, the minimum distance, and the coverage area for PAC codes. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between the number of input symbols and the code's error-correction capabilities, establishing a lower bound for the average number of correctable errors. This lower bound indicates that PAC codes can achieve an average number of correctable errors that is linear with respect to the number of input symbols. This is a distinctive feature among error-correction codes. We also discuss two approaches to calculate the error-correction performance - measurement and computation. Measurement involves analyzing the code's performance based on its geometric characteristics, whereas computation relies on numerical methods to evaluate the code's performance for specific data sets. We examine both methods and provide a new algorithm to evaluate the code's performance for continuous data sets. This algorithm is particularly useful for evaluating codes that use metrics based on angular measures, such as the Bhattacharjee code. We apply this algorithm to the PAC code and present its performance in terms of the average correction capability for various data sets. This paper also explores the relationship between pulse-addition codes and vector error-correction codes, proposing a generalization of the pulse-addition code and examining its performance. Finally, we provide a MATLAB code for implementing the algorithm and generating plots of the average correction capability for the PAC code. This code is available online. Tuning the hyperparameters of transformation-based models, which are considered to have an extensive action space due to their sequence-to-sequence nature, is challenging because of their high computational costs. Despite the difficulties, we've found that reinforcement learning can effectively optimize these models, leading to a 10% improvement in translation accuracy as measured by BLEU score. To further expand on this success, we've developed a robust framework for incorporating action costs in reinforcement learning, which helps neural machine translation models focus on high-quality actions by assigning high costs to unnecessary actions like padding tokens. We've tested this framework on multiple datasets and found that it leads to improved performance, with a 5% increase in BLEU score visible in challenging data sets. The code for our proposed method is available at https://github.com/ghrua/RL-TS.

The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly captivating, and these systems may exhibit intriguing properties like non-zero sum currents of reservoirs interacting with them. This study examines a periodic driven qubit in a thermal environment and investigates both theoretically and empirically the steady-state condition it approaches. Theoretical calculations predict the emergence of two distinct stable states, separated by a critical temperature where the driving force's frequency matches the qubit's energy gap. These predictions include accurate measurements of two-way population flows and the average energy of the qubit. A precise comparison between theoretical and experimental findings reveals that even at high temperatures, despite intense two-way interaction, not only does the qubit maintain coherence but also the stability of its steady-state condition. Additionally, the study reveals that despite being an open system, the sum of the currents between its population and environment remains zero in the steady-state condition. The research was conducted using a superconducting qubit coupled with a microwave reservoir, and involved analyzing periodic driving effects under different conditions, combining experimental outcomes with theoretical analysis of the system. The complex data was further understood through numerical simulation of the time-series. The investigation into a single-photon driven system also uncovered periodic fluctuations in the qubit's population and average energy, along with sudden cessation of coherent oscillations when the driving force's frequency aligns with the qubit's energy gap. The study into a continuous driving system revealed various interesting phenomena, including the system's ability to continuously transfer and retain entropy, and the influence of temperature on its stability. The findings have significant implications for developing robust quantum systems that can maintain coherence and stability even at high temperatures, and for understanding the intricate relationship between open and driven quantum systems. The research into a continuous driving system also uncovered novel attributes, and the study into a single-photon driven system uncovered periodic fluctuations in the qubit's population and energy, along with the cessation of coherent oscillations when the driving force's frequency aligns with the qubit's energy gap. The study into a single-photon driven system further showed that despite being an open system, the sum of the currents between its population and environment remains zero in the steady-state condition, and the complex data was further understood through numerical simulation of the time-series. The investigation into a continuous driving system revealed various interesting phenomena, including the system's ability to continuously transfer and retain entropy, and the influence of temperature on its stability. The study into a continuous driving system also uncovered novel attributes, and the findings have significant implications for developing robust quantum systems that can maintain coherence

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented NoSQL database that has gained
significant popularity in recent years. Despite its success, MongoDB's
transactional functionality remains understudied in the database research
community. This paper addresses this gap by delving into the validation of
MongoDB's transactional integrity in relation to its document-based data model.
Specifically, we examine the concept of referential integrity, which is an
essential feature across various databases. However, referential integrity is
particularly challenging to enforce in MongoDB due to its document-oriented
structure, where relationships between data entities are established through
inter-document connections rather than foreign keys. We detail our approach to
validate MongoDB's referential integrity by utilizing a theory of structured
documents and a formulation of database operations as transitions between
states. Furthermore, we illustrate how to implement referential integrity as a
property of the database state and provide a theoretical basis for its validation
through a formal method called model checking. In the course of our analysis,
we identify an incompatibility between MongoDB's document data model and the
traditional concept of referential integrity, namely the impossibility of
enforcing an integrity constraint on a relationship between documents that have
different structures. In the process, we examine various types of database
relationships and the appropriate forms of their expression in MongoDB, as
well as the challenges of validating referential integrity in relation to the
database's B-tree storage structure. Additionally, we offer a solution to this
incompatibility challenge by modifying the data model to include foreign keys,
and demonstrate how to validate the integrity of relationships in this new model. 
Finally, we conclude by discussing our research's broader implications and its
potential utility as a foundation for further work on the specification and
validation of MongoDB's transactional integrity. This research was conducted
as part of a larger project aimed at developing a framework for the
specification and validation of NoSQL database transactions, and we believe it
may also be relevant to other document-oriented databases that share MongoDB's
data model and transactional semantics. This paper presents our findings in a
clear, self-contained manner, with the underlying project context implicitly
integrated into the text.

Thanks to speech-emotion-based applications such as intelligent traffic management and customer service systems, detecting emotions in speech has become a popular area of research. Although deep learning-based models have achieved high accuracy in speech-emotion classification, their performance suffers when adapting to new domains with limited data. A recent paper provides an analysis of advancements made in categorizing monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with rational potential properties. A specific subset of potential properties is studied which comprise generalized Hermite polynomials, constructed through the use of Wronskians from standard Hermite polynomials, often seen in mathematical physics and random matrix theories. This class of quadratic potentials displays oscillatory behavior near the origin and we establish an explicit condition to determine non-singularity, including an assessment of localization with respect to polynomial index and the location of zeros within the complex plane. Furthermore, one-dimensional Supersymmetric Quantum Mechanics reveals that non-singular potentials arise from combining the harmonic oscillator with polynomial versions of Heisenberg's ladder operators, effectively encapsulating generalized Hermite polynomials through periodic closure, leading to solutions to the Painlevé IV equation and revealing a connection between Schrödinger operator discrete spectra and the monodromy-free property. Additionally, we demonstrate that the property of having non-singular potentials is stable under nearness measures, both with respect to the index and zero location, whereas the property of having localized potentials is not, resulting in the derivation of models exhibiting transition from non-singular to localized potential properties, including models with periodic oscillations between these two properties. Lastly, a comparison with potentials derived from random matrix theories, specifically the Dyson beta-ensemble, is presented. This work is composed of three sections with original contributions, including the categorization of generalized Hermite polynomial potentials based on zero location and index, the stability of these properties, and the derivation of models exhibiting transition between these properties, and the analysis of one-dimensional Supersymmetric Quantum Mechanics revealing non-singular potentials, and the connection to the Painlevé IV equation and stability of these properties in the space of possible generalized Hermite polynomials. The paper also surveys existing results on this class of potential properties, including the relation to the monodromy-free property, the stability of these properties in the complex plane, and the derivation of models exhibiting transition between these properties, and the analysis of one-dimensional Supersymmetric Quantum Mechanics revealing non-singular potentials, and the connection to the Painlevé IV equation and stability of these properties in the space of possible generalized Hermite polynomials. This research explores the mechanism by which prospects for social mobility are shared among different generations and examines the effects on present and future generations' economic behavior. Our analysis reveals that the current generation's willingness to invest in future social mobility is influenced by its own opportunities and those available to its parents. Conversely, the level of investment made in future social mobility does not impact the opportunities of great-grandchildren. Furthermore, we find that the distribution of investment in future social mobility is characterized by a decreasing pattern across successive generations. Our research also discovers that the over-cautious behavior exhibited by generations that experience reduced social mobility leads to a decline in investment in future social mobility, resulting in a sharp decline in prospects for their distant descendants. Our study further finds that this over-cautious behavior can lead to a cumulative effect, causing the decline in prospects to deepen across generations. Our findings are robust and we observe similar outcomes in different scenarios. Our research provides policy-relevant insights, demonstrating that interventions designed to enhance the economic well-being of the current generation will eventually benefit future generations. We also examine the implications of such interventions for the distribution of prospects across different generations and find that they lead to a more even distribution of prospects. Our research further finds that the most effective way to increase investment in future social mobility is through taxation systems that target the wealthy, specifically progressive taxation systems. We also examine the outcomes of different taxation systems and find that they lead to a more even distribution of prospects across different generations. Our research provides a historical context for the outcomes observed, examining the distribution of prospects in different societies and finding that the distribution of prospects varies significantly across these societies. We find that the most extreme outcomes are characterized by the extreme over-cautious behavior exhibited by generations that experience reduced social mobility, leading to a decline in prospects for their distant descendants. Our research provides a theoretical framework for understanding the distribution of prospects in a dynamic framework of intergenerational mobility and examines the outcomes of different scenarios within this framework, finding that the distribution of prospects is shaped by the interactions between different generations and the economic and social laws that govern these interactions. We find that the distribution of prospects can be altered through interventions designed to change the way different generations interact with each other, providing a roadmap for developing such interventions. This paper describes the method used to analyze the beam size of the x-ray beam at the ID-29 beamline at ESRF. To precisely determine the vertical size of the x-ray beam, a horizontal scan is performed in front of a detector placed perpendicular to the beam, and the resulting data is analyzed using a Gaussian fit. The vertical beam size is then calculated as the standard deviation of this fit, with an accuracy of 1% achieved through repeated measurements. The method has been successfully utilized to monitor changes in beam size over time and to evaluate the effects of different optical elements and their positions within the beamline. Furthermore, this approach can be applied to determine the beam characteristics at other synchrotron facilities with similar beamline configurations. The associated software is available for public use. The accuracy of this method has also been validated using a customized Monte Carlo simulation using the GEMC code. The current version of the software can be found at the GitHub repository https://github.com/ESRF-ID/Beam-Size-Scanner. The code is written in Python 2 and utilizes the matplotlib library for data visualization. The associated scanner hardware is composed of a precise stepping motor, a high-speed area detector, and a computer system, and it allows for automatic data collection and subsequent analysis. The development of the hardware and software for this beam scan system is ongoing, with future improvements aimed at enhancing the data collection process, implementing real-time data analysis, and integrating it with the ESRF control system. The current version of the hardware is suited for offline use, but it has the potential to be adapted for online beam analysis at other facilities with similar beamline configurations. We reveal the assaulter's optimal strategy and the resulting system-wide cost. To overcome this challenge, we develop a robust gradient update algorithm, ensuring that each worker protects their dataset from assault. We then investigate realistic scenarios in which some workers may assault the algorithm, and we develop a distributed optimization algorithm to minimize system-wide cost while ensuring that each worker maintains control over its own dataset. Finally, we provide numerical evidence to demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm in various scenarios. In conclusion, this research addresses the issue of malicious assault in a context where a system performs optimization on data contributed by various workers. We have developed a robust gradient algorithm capable of withstanding data manipulation by some workers, and we have shown that in a simplified scenario, this algorithm leads to costs similar to those of non-robust methods, while in a more complex scenario, it offers tangible benefits, as shown by numerical examples. In this research, we delve into the mechanics of linguistic models, specifically pre-trained language models, to better understand their capabilities in arranging words into meaningful phrases. A case study with BART, a state-of-the-art model, reveals that it relies on either semantic or syntactic analysis to arrange words, or a combination of both. To gain this insight, we systematically mistrained BART to exclusively use either semantic or syntactic analysis for arrangement tasks, and then evaluated its performance. Our findings show that BART primarily uses a combination of semantic and syntactic analysis to arrange words, although it favors semantic analysis. It particularly excels at arrangement tasks that rely heavily on semantic analysis, such as combining word pairs with the same meaning, yet it struggles with tasks that rely heavily on syntactic analysis, such as constructing complex sentences from simple ones. Our research also uncovers a phenomenon called overfitting in BART, where it becomes overly familiar with common phrase structures and accordingly overfits them. As a result, we propose methods to prevent overfitting and significantly improve BART's performance in arrangement tasks. One way to achieve this is by incorporating random sentence reordering into our training data, which we call "Semantic Sentence Reordering" (SSR). Another approach is by utilizing a less complex model, which we found to be more effective at preventing overfitting. Our evaluation shows that both of these methods are highly successful in preventing overfitting and improving BART's performance in arrangement tasks. One interesting aspect of our research is the observation that BART arranges words based on their local semantic analysis, rather than their global context. To validate this finding, we developed an automated tool to visually depict the level of local vs. global context used by BART in arrangement tasks, which we call the Context Map. Our analysis of BART's Context Maps reveals that it uses local context more extensively than global context, and that there is a positive correlation between the level of global context used and arrangement task difficulty. Moreover, our evaluation shows that both of the methods we proposed, SSR and the less complex model, result in BART using a higher level of global context in arrangement tasks. One possible application of our research is in building more intelligent chatbots that can engage in natural language conversations with humans. The rapid dissemination of deepfake media poses a significant challenge to information authenticity and spreads false information that can influence public opinion and cause harm to individuals. As a result, developing an highly efficient and robust deepfake detection system for real-time use is crucial. Current deepfake detection methods primarily rely on artificial intelligence models that rely on training and testing data, without giving sufficient consideration to the source attribution of manipulated media. This limitation allows adversaries to create deceptive evidence that denies responsibility for the alteration of a particular piece of media. To address this issue, researchers have introduced new standards that require artificial intelligence models to accurately identify the degree to which a piece of data has been modified based on training data that includes both clean and deeply fabricated samples. Although there has been significant progress in developing artificial intelligence models to detect deepfakes, research on this topic has largely been conducted within the confines of a controlled laboratory setting. To further evaluate the effectiveness of these models, it is essential to conduct empirical studies on their ability to meet these new standards in real-world scenarios. Additionally, there is a need for more innovative approaches that prioritize the attribution of manipulated data and consider the perspectives of different stakeholders involved in the discovery and dissemination of deepfake media. To address these challenges, we propose a novel network architecture called the MD-CSDNetwork that specializes in detecting deepfakes and estimating the level to which a piece of data has been modified, and we present a comprehensive empirical study that evaluates this network and other artificial intelligence models based on a newly created dataset that reflects real-world conditions and multiple perspectives. Our findings indicate that the MD-CSDNetwork significantly outperforms other artificial intelligence models across the board and our analysis reveals that the dispersal of deepfake media on social media platforms is driven by the intention to spread false information that has a harmful impact on individuals. Our research opens up new avenues for improving artificial intelligence models based on contrasting training data, and we offer a straightforward method for building such models. Furthermore, our findings provide a much-needed understanding of the spread of deepfake media and the stakeholders involved, and we offer a new standard for evaluating artificial intelligence models based on the perspective of the individuals whose identities are being misrepresented. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghrghr81/MDCSDNetwork.

The catalog of the Milky Way bulge globular clusters compiled by Ornitelli et al. (2020) was tested using photometric and kinematic data from the VVV survey. In recent years, adversarial text generation techniques have undergone significant development. A important application of text generation includes creating large datasets for various text-based AI systems, such as chatbots and virtual assistants, that can engage in conversation with humans. Currently, text generation models can produce responses to a single input sentence, but they lack the ability to create multiple relevant sentences. To address this limitation, we present SparseGAN, a novel sparse generative adversary network that produces a concise set of diverse sentence options. Unlike traditional generative adversary networks, SparseGAN has two opposing roles: a generator that devises plausible sentences and an adversary that discriminates between authentic and artificially created sentences based on a given context. The generator aims to create artificial sentences that can deceive the adversary and stimulate meaningful language generation. Conversely, the adversary strives to differentiate between genuine and artificially generated sentences and, in the process, develops a deep understanding of the target language. We incorporate two opposing roles for the adversary as a combined operation where the generator outputs a dense set of sentences and the adversary receives a dense vector representing the likelihood of each sentence. We demonstrate SparseGAN's effectiveness in generating high-quality sentence options by conducting a set of extensive experiments on various text generation tasks. The code for SparseGAN is publicly available at https://github.com/sigwen/SparseGAN.

Animal population studies often aim to assess the health and conservation status of species.  A method called Spatial Capture-Recapture (SCR) uses encounter data from animals interacting with each other and their environment to estimate population characteristics.  SCR analysis incorporates encounter probability models to weigh the importance of capture locations and animal characteristics.  However, SCR primarily focuses on demographic information and may not account for factors influencing animals' choice of resources.  A new method, Resource-SCR, combines SCR and resource choice models to also estimate the factors that guide animals' habitat use.  Resource-SCR evaluates capture locations' relevance to estimating resource choice models and weights them accordingly.  By integrating capture data with knowledge of the environment and the animals that use it, Resource-SCR provides a richer understanding of animal populations and can inform more effective conservation strategies.  We apply and evaluate Resource-SCR using data from white-tailed deer studied in a capture-recapture project.  The evaluation shows that Resource-SCR accurately estimates the factors influencing deer habitat use and offers a way to account for capture location bias.  We also explore Resource-SCR's performance when studying deer on larger scales.  In doing so, we discover that Resource-SCR's capture location-weighting model can be an alternative to SCR's spatial model when studying larger areas.  Finally, we discuss ways to enhance Resource-SCR and a related R package called rscrc, which is available online. Recent advancements in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in patients with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body recovery but have yet to achieve successful restoration of lower body mobility. A major limitation in addressing this issue has been the lack of understanding regarding how the central nervous system controls ambulatory states and step cycles. This study addresses this knowledge gap by analyzing high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of individuals with complete spinal cord injuries attempting to walk within a virtual reality environment. Unusual approaches were taken to extract the step frequencies from the recorded data by applying techniques typically used for analyzing time series data and comparing them to previous methods used for determining the walk-state probability. Results showed that step frequencies could be accurately determined using both approaches, and that different state frequency models could predict walk-state probability with a high degree of accuracy. Furthermore, a notable discrepancy was observed between the frequencies associated with walk states and other ambulatory states, suggesting that the central nervous system encodes this information in the form of step frequencies. This study provides novel insights into the underlying mechanisms of the central nervous system's control over step cycles and walks, and has implications for designing more effective BCIs that could recover lower body mobility in patients with spinal cord injuries. Moreover, the findings have broader applications in fields beyond BCI, such as sports and dance, by shedding light on the complex temporal dynamics of the central nervous system during physical activities. The code and data associated with this study are available for public use. The findings presented in this study have been theoretically validated but further experimental verification is necessary. The proposed approach can be improved by addressing issues related to the quality of the ECoG recordings, the complexity of the frequency models, and the limited duration of the walk states. Observing dogs and their interactions with their environments is also a popular recreation for many people worldwide.  Many videos feature dogs moving naturally in various settings, including parks, homes, and outdoor spaces.  Due to the free movement of the dogs within these environments, their paths cannot be predicted preensively.  As a result, detecting biologically generated motion in videos of dogs has become a crucial task.  Currently, most methods treat the underlying motion as unknown and concentrate on detecting syntactic features instead.  On the other hand, research on birds has established reference standards for the motion patterns associated with their flights.  By extending this approach to dogs, researchers have defined movement standards based on their observable behaviors.  These movements include tail wagging, running, walking, and jumping.  By utilizing these reference standards, various evaluation metrics can be employed to assess the motion-related content of videos featuring dogs.  Moreover, incorporating these standards into machine learning models enables the automatic detection of biologically generated movement in videos, a task that can also be performed using alternative approaches such as optimization methods. This ROI optimization method is compatible with the reference standards and provides a straightforward yet effective solution for detecting the motion patterns of dogs.  This approach can also be tailored to suit the needs of other species by establishing reference movement standards for their individual behaviors. Our research reinvestigates initial condition models used in relativistic heavy-ion collisions, specifically for inclusive particle distributions, with a focus on the event shape variable elliptic flow ($v_2$) at a center-of-mass energy of 2.76 TeV through relativistic hydrodynamic simulations. Initial conditions were derived from three models with different property assumptions: long-range elliptic flow fluctuation patterns derived from collective fluid dynamics, partially coherent stochastic field configurations based on the Gubser mechanism, and homogeneous initial state properties obtained by applying the 4π integral over the initial energy-density distribution. Our analysis shows that the average $v_2$ coefficients for the $\pi$, $K^*$, and $K$ mesons and the $\Lambda$ and $\bar{\Lambda}$ baryons differ significantly, with an observed response to the event shape distribution that contradicts our current understanding. The results also imply that the majority of the observed $v_2$ relies on inherent properties of the medium rather than initial condition fluctuations, and that the primary contributing factor to $v_2$ is related to specific average initial condition properties that are readily accessible in experiments and simulations. Consequently, we propose a new event shape distribution-based approach that may serve as a precise probe of the medium's properties and is applicable to a broad range of systems and collisions. Furthermore, our findings highlight the significance of $v_2$ distributions in identifying quark hadronization and the $v_2$ coefficient's sensitivity to the medium's temperature and the underlying physics that drives hadronization. Lastly, we discuss the implications of our research for the fundamental theories of quantum chromodynamics, the hadronization process, and the properties of the medium, and we propose a range of related experimental and theoretical studies that could significantly advance our understanding of heavy-ion collisions.

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate through deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on the control system development for a one-legged jumping robot, specifically designed to jump onto various types of soft terrain, including foam and sand. A novel approach was taken to model terrain dynamics by considering ground state estimation instead of attempting to fully comprehend the complex dynamics of ground deformation. The effect of ground deformation on the leg was represented by contact force generation using a layer that integrated force and position information. A hybrid model was developed to accommodate this approach, and it showed improved performance in simulating ground reaction forces in comparison to other methods. The control system developed in this project allowed the one-legged jumping robot to successfully land on soft terrain. However, issues were encountered with foot slippage, which necessitate the integration of more sophisticated state estimation techniques to enhance safety and overall performance. The simulation code has been made available online for further development and improvement. This research was conducted in collaboration with the LegLab group at Cornell University. The findings have been published in the paper referenced below.

Quantum annealing within a suitable interval proves effective in solving Ising complement problems, even when thermal errors affect the process. However, there's a lack of understanding regarding the conditions under which quantum annealing excels. This study investigates the quantum annealing interval, revealing that it's composed of two sections: one where the success probability decreases gradually, and a second section where the probability drops off more rapidly. We also examine non-equilibrium dynamics in this problem. When the system is not fully furnished with sufficient quantum resources, heat-bath spectral density converges as the size of the system increases. Conversely, when the system has ample quantum resources, heat-bath spectral density rises in proportion to the system's size. This research provides a new perspective on non-equilibrium dynamics, centered on temporal evolution rather than static properties. By redefining average success probability through temporal averaging, we discover that heat-bath spectral density rises in proportion to the system's size in the quantum annealing regime where thermal errors prevail. This indicates that temporal averaging is a more sensitive indicator of thermal errors in this regime. We also discover that the effective quantum annealing interval increases in proportion to the square root of the system's size. This research was applied to the precise cover problem in biology, namely reconstructing genomes from gene coverage data. When the number of non-overlapping genes isn't sufficiently large, this data can be represented by Ising complements, otherwise it's represented by an exact cover problem. We presented a novel, efficient solution for this problem, along with simulated results using quantum annealing. These simulations demonstrated that the quantum annealing interval increases in proportion to the square root of the number of non-overlapping genes, and that heat-bath spectral density rises in proportion to the number of genes. This research also discussed various biological scenarios, namely the minimum number of non-overlapping genes required, the depth of the genome reconstruction tree, the distribution of gene lengths, and the number of reads per gene base. To create more realistic chatbots, our goal is to build a system that generates human-like responses to everyday questions by drawing on general knowledge. While significant progress has been made in developing such systems, they often struggle with more abstract and logically complex questions that require a deeper understanding of relationships and concepts. To improve these models, we believe it's necessary to focus on capturing the underlying connections between concepts and addressing the inherent ambiguity present in everyday language. To this end, we propose a method for constructing a concept graph that represents the interconnections between the entities mentioned in a question and provides a way to evaluate the generated response based on this graph, ensuring the response is both semantically connected to the question and logically consistent. We've tested this approach on two datasets that evaluate the complexity of question concepts, and our results show that it outperforms the current state-of-the-art approaches. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghru/CCIQA.

A systematic investigation has been conducted to analyze the existing spectral data of composite molecular cations containing oxygen. These data are crucial for interpreting the spectral patterns of comets, especially in the UV and visible spectrum range, where ring systems of planets like Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars might lack spectral evidence. A comprehensive database of composite molecular cations containing oxygen was created, based on sources such as scientific literature, molecular databases, and theoretical spectroscopic simulations. This database was then compared to a comprehensive list of known molecular cations, with a focus on those that feature oxygen and have been studied through theoretical spectroscopic means. The comparison revealed that many of these cations have limited or no recorded spectral data, especially in the visible spectrum range. Certain cations like HOC+, NO2+, CO2+, HNCO+, and HN2+ have limited recorded spectral data, often in the form of band strengths rather than detailed spectral patterns. On the other hand, a small group of cations like H2O+, OH+, O2+, and NO+ have more comprehensive recorded spectral data, with some even having previous comet detection claims. Despite the importance of these cations in understanding and interpreting the spectral patterns of planets and comets, especially in the UV and visible spectrum range, more extensive research is needed to fully capture their spectral characteristics. Such research could involve combining and matching recorded and simulated spectroscopic data, along with experimenting with different theoretical approaches to better predict their behavior and spectral patterns. If achieved, it could provide a more complete and accurate picture of the molecular composition of comets and planets through remote spectral analysis. The created database is available for further study and can be accessed through the Planetary Data System. This paper introduces the Random Stroll Method (RSM) to address challenges in Federated Learning (FL) across diverse data. Since data heterogeneity leads to significant performance degradation in traditional FL methods, RSM was created to overcome this obstacle. The algorithm first gathers individual data sets from collaborating parties, determines the total data distribution, generates a random distribution that represents the ideal data distribution, and then uses this distribution to sort the data sets. Next, the RSM selects more representative data points from each set based on the random distribution, performs sampling on these points, and uses them to update the model. The advantages of RSM are its simplicity and efficiency as well as its compatibility with the existing FL framework. Experimental results show that RSM outperforms other baseline methods in various scenarios. The algorithm is suitable for real-world applications in social media platforms, online crowdsourcing, and multi-task learning. The code for RSM is available at https://github.com/lingwei0811/Random_Stroll_Method. The ideal random stroll criterion can also be applied in other machine learning tasks such as oversampling the minority class in imbalanced classification. The code has been tested on multiple scenarios including classification, regression, and robust learning. The paper contributes a novel perspective on learning from diverse data, a common occurrence in real-world applications. The paper discusses the relationship between data heterogeneity and learning difficulty, a novel approach that combines the distribution of individual data sets and the ideal data distribution, a novel perspective on the bias of the model, and a method for evaluating the diversity of data sets. The paper presents a theoretical analysis of the stability of the RSM, proves that RSM is compatible with the existing FL framework, and explains the performance of RSM in contrast to the baseline methods. The paper discusses various challenging scenarios in FL, a multi-stroll method in FL, a robust learning method in FL, a crowdsourcing learning model in FL, a model in multi-task learning, a model in social media learning, a method for evaluating the diversity of data sets, a method for oversampling the minority class in imbalanced classification, a method for evaluating the complexity of the model, and a method for evaluating the randomness of the data sets. Creating effective proof systems for SMT solvers involves a delicate balance in designing a format that is both convenient for users and soluble for verifiers. A perfect solution likely doesn't exist as different solvers have distinct design philosophies, evidence formats, and varying capabilities to generate or verify proofs. Our experiments reveal that the majority of solvers already generate soluble proofs for the existing SMT constraint language, and that a significant number of solvers can be easily integrated with the Alethe framework by simply switching to a more transparent proof format, given that many solvers' evidence generation mechanisms are already quite transparent. We also examine the challenge of solvers that employ complex proof generation methods and propose potential avenues for integrating them with Alethe. Ultimately, our work takes the initial step towards creating a universal standard for SMT proof languages, one that can be used by a diverse range of solvers, and provides a practical solution for users who only need a limited subset of the verifiers listed in our solvers collection. The evidence formats and solvers used in this study have been made publicly available.

The notion that entanglement between two particles is necessary for true nonlocality to arise has been a long-standing misconception. Our calculation demonstrates that a single particle, despite being unentangled with respect to a particular measurement basis, can still exhibit nonlocal behavior when interacting with a quantum system. This scenario, characterized by a non-zero correlation between the particle's state and the system's outcome, cannot be replicated through local actions alone. Consequently, it compels the particle to follow a guided path, demonstrating nonlocal influence that is essentially entanglement-free. This finding serves as a direct extension of the EPR paradox and the GHZ theorem, offering a tangible, experimentally verifiable manifestation of nonlocality that can be implemented in various quantum systems. Although our primary example involves a qutrit, this effect is universally applicable to any multi-level quantum system, regardless of its complexity. It can be implemented in both continuous and discrete variable systems, as well as in spatial, entanglement-based, or contextuality-based nonlocality scenarios. Our analysis also explores various ways in which this effect can be manipulated, including through unitary operations, measurement bases, and the presence or absence of entanglement. Our research highlights the importance of considering multiple measurement bases to accurately assess a system's nonlocal properties, demonstrating that a failure to do so can lead to the misclassification of a system as nonlocal when it actually is not. This finding has implications for ongoing experiments aimed at detecting nonlocality in systems like trapped ions, Bose-Einstein condensates, and spin-orbit coupled atoms, and provides a straightforward approach to generating nonlocal behavior in these systems. It also offers a novel means of generating contextuality, which is a fundamental property of quantum mechanics, in systems like the Gell-Mann Tomberg effect. Our research concludes by proposing a realistic, high-accuracy experiment designed to directly detect nonlocal behavior in a system of three trapped ions. This experiment involves a setup where a single particle's state is guided by a quantum system located at a distant site, forcing it to choose a particular state in accordance with the outcome of a measurement made on another site, with the effect being durable enough to survive multiple re-preparations of the initial state. It can be carried out using existing technology, with a success probability of over 90%, and would mark the first detection of nonlocal behavior in a system of three trapped ions, as well as providing a means of generating contextuality and entanglement in a continuous variable system.

In FDD systems, codebook design and feedback encoding are critical components that greatly impact the performance and mobility of the antenna configuration. Codebooks are often constructed using Gaussian random matrices, which, however, result in suboptimal performance due to the inaccurate modeling of measured GMMs. This paper presents a novel approach to designing codebooks and feedback encoding schemes based on the measured GMMs of antenna configurations, which provides better performance while maintaining practical computation requirements. Specifically, an overcomplete codebook is constructed using GMM-based clustering, and then a reduced codebook is created by selecting the most representative vectors from the overcomplete codebook. Furthermore, a threshold-based feedback encoding scheme is proposed to increase the efficiency of data transmission. The proposed approach was verified to outperform traditional methods in various scenarios. The codebook and feedback encoding scheme were implemented in a 4x4 FDD system using an OFDM modulator, and the results showed significant performance improvements over conventional methods. The codebook and feedback encoding scheme were also found to be highly adaptive to different antenna configurations and environments. The paper concludes by highlighting the practical applications and potential areas for further research in FDD systems. Despite the simplicity of their text-based interface, these games pose significant challenges for the latest advanced models, which have been largely tested against them. The pace at which users interact with texts and actions are translated into responses limits the scale of current experiments, making it difficult to conduct thorough evaluations. To address this issue, we present TextWorldExpress, a high-performance virtual environment that can simulate text games at an incredible rate of over one million steps per second on a single GPU, and allows for the easy creation of large-scale evaluation datasets and complex agent training datasets. We demonstrate TextWorldExpress's capabilities by generating two distinct datasets of text games, and show that our engine can efficiently handle large-scale agent evaluations and training data by achieving a 12-fold decrease in evaluation time and a 6-fold decrease in training time for state-of-the-art models. TextWorldExpress, a powerful tool for the community, is available open-source. Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have achieved high accuracy in video recognition tasks but suffer from high computational costs and large memory requirements, making them less practical for mobile applications. To address this issue, a new LSTM structure called Hierarchical Tucker LSTMs (HTLSTMs) is proposed that combines the benefits of hardware efficiency and high model accuracy. The proposed HTLSTMs algorithm utilizes a hierarchical tensor decomposition technique to reduce computational and memory costs and implements a rolling forecasting strategy to minimize waste computation. Furthermore, a high-speed hardware implementation platform based on Hierarchical Tucker LSTMs is developed, featuring 16 LSTMs modules, 16 fully connected modules, and a controller, and includes a precision selection mechanism and a data loading module to increase efficiency. The HTLSTMs algorithm and hardware co-design outperform standard LSTM models in terms of energy consumption, area occupancy, and accuracy, and can be applied to various time-series prediction tasks in addition to video recognition. The HTLSTMs hardware platform has a core area of 0.038 mm2, can process 25 frames per second, and has an energy consumption of 0.64 nJ per inference, making it suitable for mobile applications. The accuracy of HTLSTMs is evaluated on the UCF101 and HMDB51 datasets and the results show that it outperforms standard LSTM models and other energy-efficient LSTM structures. The proposed HTLSTMs algorithm and hardware co-development can be expanded to other mobile deep learning applications. Additionally, we provide a counterexample to show that this proportionality no longer holds when the polynomials and their iterates do share a root. Furthermore, we offer a more specific instance of a polynomial that exhibits this behavior associated with a particular point, and we demonstrate that any transformation or change in basis does not alter this property. Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by powerful, long-lasting vortex patterns that mimic those found on Jupiter. The formation of these polar vortices during the solstices defines Saturn's unique polar atmosphere phenomenon. Until now, research has focused on the southern polar region due to its prolonged summer conditions. This study uses recently available clear-filter images from the Cassini spacecraft to examine the southern polar region during its approach to summer. The increasing temperature and decreasing atmospheric pressure with altitude create obstacles to detecting the developing polar vortex in the north following the end of the winter solstice. However, examining the southern pole during its approach to equinox, a time of rapid temperature and pressure changes, proves feasible. One notable feature in the southern pole is a developing hexagonal storm with sides approximately 8700 kilometers long, which is surrounded by an expanding polar vortex. Distinguishable edges on this hexagon are notable for their sharp curvature, suggesting they are caused by the same type of shear layer present on a much smaller scale within the north polar vortex. The decreasing pressure with altitude in the outer region of the hexagon's wind pattern is also observed for the first time, a feature previously seen only in the northern pole. The growing polar vortex in the southern pole occurs when the sun's rays begin shining directly on the tropics rather than the poles, a time when the temperature and pressure gradients with altitude are at their most extreme. This leads to the formation of a prominent polar vortex when the sun shines directly on the poles, a result that has been theoretically predicted but not previously proven. This study highlights the importance of further research on the developing summer vortex, and suggests northern pole observations could be more feasible with a shorter wavelength filter that penetrates higher altitudes. This would involve obtaining images during the earliest hours of the summer, when the temperature and pressure gradients with altitude are at their most extreme, a time when the developing summer vortex is most easily detected. This could provide a deeper understanding of the formation of the northern pole's permanent vortex, and reveal a similar expanding shear layer and increasing curvature on the outer storm boundaries, which are absent in the inner regions of the hexagon wind patterns. This would also reveal the initial stage of the northern pole's vortex formation, which is the opposite of the changing conditions found in the southern pole during equinox. This could be detected by examining the inner regions of the hexagon wind patterns for the decreasing temperature and increasing pressure with altitude, a time when the sun's rays begin shining directly on the poles rather than the tropics.

Additionally, we provide a map that maps a polynomial algebra to the algebra generated by its set of variables, and show that this map is natural and induces a monomorphism on its underlying collection. However, we also find that this map is not an epimorphism, and it is not compatible with the structure of a coordinate algebra. Moreover, we discover that it is possible to extend the polarized collection of a module algebra to become a coordinate algebra, and provide a criterion for this extension to be unique. Furthermore, we find that this approach is applicable to the polarized collection of a module over a field, and it leads to the development of a division algorithm for its polynomial ring. Lastly, we explore the relationship between the polarized collection of a module algebra and its coordinate algebra, and it leads to the discovery of a ring theorem that is more general than a well-known criterion for a ring to be a coordinate ring. Lastly, we clarify the relationship between the polarized collection of a module algebra and its coordinate algebra, and it leads to the development of a division algorithm for its polynomial ring, and it also results in a ring theorem that is capable of being applied to a wide range of coordinate rings.
